title: The classical cosmological models
one_line_summary: Integrates the dust Friedmann equation for the flat and Λ = 0 cases, sorts every (k, Λ) combination into a catalogue of scale-factor histories, then studies the special solutions (Einstein static, de Sitter, radiation-filled, steady state), cosmological horizons, the Lorentzian spaces of constant curvature (de Sitter and anti-de Sitter) as embedded hyperboloids, the Penrose diagrams of all of these, and ends with a qualitative inflation-radiation-matter-vacuum history.
role_in_book: Middle chapter of the book's three-chapter cosmology part. Chapter 24 built the Robertson-Walker metric, derived Friedmann's equation for dust, and defined redshift, luminosity distance, Hubble and deceleration parameters; this chapter takes that equation as given and solves it, turning abstract parameters (C, Λ, k) into explicit histories R(t). It then reuses the global-structure machinery of Chapter 18 (conformal compactification onto the Einstein static cylinder, Penrose diagrams) and the horizon ideas of Chapters 3 and 17 to describe the causal structure of cosmological spacetimes. It closes with a qualitative history of the universe that sets up Chapter 26, where multi-component models, observations, ΛCDM and inflation are treated properly.

assumed_background.topic: Friedmann's equation for pressure-free matter, with constant C = (8/3)πR³ρ
Einstein equations for a Robertson-Walker perfect fluid and the energy equation d(ρR³)/dt + p d(R³)/dt = 0
Robertson-Walker line element with curvature index k = -1, 0, +1
Spaces of constant curvature and the 3-geometries of the spatial slices (χ radial coordinate)
Light propagation along radial null geodesics, cosmological redshift, luminosity and geodesic distance
Hubble parameter H = Ṙ/R and deceleration parameter q = -RR̈/Ṙ²
The cosmological term and the sign convention G_ab - Λg_ab = 8πT_ab
Conformal compactification, the Einstein static cylinder metric (18.27), scri and Penrose diagram of Minkowski space-time
Event horizon of a uniformly accelerated observer in special relativity
Riemann, Ricci and Einstein tensors with the book's sign conventions and signature (+,-,-,-)
Integration by substitution with trigonometric and hyperbolic functions; separable first-order ODEs
Qualitative analysis of one-dimensional motion from an energy equation (turning points where the 'kinetic' term vanishes)
Quadric surfaces (hyperboloids) in flat spaces of indefinite signature
Radiation equation of state p = ρ/3 for an ultra-relativistic gas
Observed galaxy recession (Slipher, Hubble) and Hubble's law

learning_objectives: Reader can integrate the dust Friedmann equation in closed form for k = 0 with Λ > 0, Λ = 0, Λ < 0 and for Λ = 0 with k = ±1, choosing the substitution that makes each integral elementary.
Reader can compute H(t) and q(t) from an explicit solution, e.g. obtain H = 2/(3t) and q = 1/2 for the Einstein-de Sitter model.
Reader can predict the qualitative shape of R(t) from Ṙ² = F(R) by locating zeros of F (turning points) and deciding which term dominates at small and at large R.
Reader can explain why every big bang model starts like R ∝ t^{2/3} (dust) or t^{1/2} (radiation) and why any Λ > 0 eventually drives exponential expansion in an ever-expanding model.

Reader can reproduce the classification of Friedmann models by k and Λ, including the critical values Λ_c = 4/(9C²) and R_c = 3C/2 for k = +1 and the named special cases (Lemaître, Einstein static, Eddington-Lemaître, bouncing, oscillating).
Reader can derive the Einstein static universe from the static Friedmann equations and state why, without Λ, a static closed universe needs negative pressure.
Reader can show that the de Sitter metric written with exponential scale factor is actually stationary, by transforming to static coordinates.
Reader can reconstruct the steady-state line element from the perfect cosmological principle and show that Hubble's law d_L = zT_0 is exact and q = -1 there.
Reader can compute the event horizon of a comoving observer in de Sitter space, the reception time and redshift of a comoving source approaching it, and interpret the divergence of both.

Reader can distinguish particle horizons, observer-dependent future event horizons and absolute (black hole) horizons, and relate their existence to whether scri-minus and scri-plus are spacelike or null.

Reader can state the constant-curvature condition, derive K = R/12 and G_ab = -3Kg_ab, and visualise de Sitter and anti-de Sitter space as hyperboloids in flat five-dimensional spaces, including which part the flat (steady-state) slicing covers.

Reader can use conformal time to map Robertson-Walker, de Sitter and anti-de Sitter spacetimes onto regions of the Einstein static cylinder and read off from Penrose diagrams that the big bang is spacelike, the steady-state patch is past-incomplete, and AdS infinity is timelike.
Reader can narrate the standard sequence inflation, radiation domination, matter domination, vacuum domination using the scalings ρ ∝ R^{-4}, R^{-3}, R^0.

teaching_approach.summary: A mathematically explicit catalogue chapter. The authors take Friedmann's equation from Chapter 24 as a black box and work it like an ODE problem: exact integrations by clever substitutions for a few representative cases, then qualitative reasoning from Ṙ² = F(R) to fill in the rest, collected into one tabular figure of sketches. The second half changes register from dynamics to geometry and causal structure: special solutions are examined for coordinate artefacts (de Sitter is stationary), horizons are derived from limits of past light cones and pictured with explorer stories, constant-curvature spacetimes are shown as hyperboloids in five dimensions, and everything is placed on the Einstein static cylinder to produce Penrose diagrams. The chapter ends with a verbal, equation-light synthesis of cosmic history.
narrative_arc: Restate Friedmann's dust equation with its parameter ranges and admit that the general solution needs elliptic functions, so restrict to representative exact cases.
Solve k = 0 for Λ > 0, Λ < 0, Λ = 0 by substitutions, meeting the Einstein-de Sitter model and its H and q.
Switch to qualitative analysis: small-R dominance gives universal t^{2/3} start, zeros of F(R) give turning points, large-R dominance gives exponential growth.
Repeat for Λ = 0 with k = ±1 (cycloid-type implicit solutions, H and q) and the qualitative G(R) argument.
Collect all cases into the classification figure, introducing the critical Λ_c and R_c for k = +1 and naming the special models.

Step back historically: static Friedmann equations show why Einstein needed Λ; the Einstein static and de Sitter models are derived and de Sitter is shown to be the late-time attractor and secretly stationary.
Add radiation pressure: equation of state, ρ ∝ R^{-4}, faster early expansion R ∝ t^{1/2}, Friedmann equation with D/R².
Present the steady-state theory from the perfect cosmological principle, recover the de Sitter metric, exact Hubble law and q = -1.

Use the same metric to derive the event horizon of a comoving observer, follow a source to the horizon (infinite redshift, recession velocity to c), tell the explorer story and compare with Rindler horizons.
Generalise to a taxonomy of particle and event horizons controlled by the character of scri-minus and scri-plus.
Treat de Sitter and anti-de Sitter as Lorentzian constant curvature spaces: embeddings, global coordinates, the half covered by flat slicing.
Conformally compactify Robertson-Walker (Λ = 0), de Sitter and anti-de Sitter onto the Einstein static cylinder and draw their Penrose diagrams; note AdS/CFT in passing.
Summarise the realistic picture: inflation, radiation, matter and vacuum eras, pointing to Chapter 26 for detail.
signature_moves: Turns an ODE whose general solution is elliptic into a small set of elementary integrals by tailored substitutions (u ∝ R³ with cosh, u² = R/C with sin), then justifies not doing the rest by showing that dominance arguments recover all qualitative shapes.

Reads dynamics off a 'Ṙ² = function of R' form exactly like a particle energy equation: zeros are turning points, dominant terms give asymptotics; Exercise 25.7 makes the Newtonian particle-in-a-channel analogy explicit.

Packs the entire model space into one grid of hand sketches (Fig. 25.1) labelled with a Roman-numeral scheme that later text refers back to (e.g. models I(i), II(i), III(i), III(iic), III(iiib) all tend to de Sitter).

Repeatedly unmasks coordinate effects: the exponentially expanding de Sitter metric is transformed into a manifestly static form; the flat slicing is shown to cover only half the hyperboloid; the periodic AdS time is unwrapped.

Obtains horizons by taking a limit of an explicit past light cone equation, then attaches physical observables (reception time, luminosity distance, redshift, geodesic recession speed) to the approach to the horizon.
Uses a narrative 'curtain' and an explorer who can see past the horizon but can never report back to make observer-dependence of event horizons vivid.
Reuses one geometric stage, the Einstein static cylinder, to draw conformal diagrams of every model, so different spacetimes become different shaded regions of the same cylinder.

sections.title: The flat space models
sections.summary: Sets the chapter's task of solving the dust Friedmann equation, then treats k = 0. For positive Λ the substitution u = 2ΛR³/(3C) and a cosh substitution give R³ proportional to cosh(√(3Λ)t) - 1; negative Λ gives the analogous 1 - cos form; Λ = 0 gives the Einstein-de Sitter model R ∝ t^{2/3} with H = 2/(3t), q = 1/2. A qualitative argument shows all big bang models start like Einstein-de Sitter, negative Λ produces a maximum radius where F(R) vanishes, and positive Λ gives exponential growth at late times.
concepts: qualitative analysis of the Friedmann equation
key_moves: Note that the general solution requires elliptic functions and restrict to k = 0 and Λ = 0 cases, citing Landsberg and Evans for completeness.
For k = 0, Λ > 0 set u = 2ΛR³/(3C) so that u̇² = 3Λ(2u + u²); complete the square, put u + 1 = cosh w and integrate with R(0) = 0 to reach (25.5).
For Λ < 0 flip the sign of the substitution to obtain the trigonometric solution (25.7).
For Λ = 0 separate R^{1/2}dR = C^{1/2}dt to get R = (9Ct²/4)^{1/3}, the Einstein-de Sitter model, and compute H = 2/(3t), q = 1/2.
Argue that near R = 0 the C/R term dominates, so every big bang model behaves as t^{2/3} initially.
Write Ṙ² = F(R) and read off: F has a zero at R_m = [3C/(-Λ)]^{1/3} when Λ < 0 (expansion halts); for Λ ≥ 0 growth is unbounded and for Λ > 0 the ΛR²/3 term gives R ∼ exp[(Λ/3)^{1/2}t].

sections.title: Models with vanishing cosmological constant
sections.summary: With Λ = 0 the equation Ṙ² = C/R - k is solved for k = +1 using u² = R/C and u = sin θ, giving an implicit cycloid-type relation between R and t; the k = -1 case gives the hyperbolic analogue. H and q are expressed as functions of R for the closed case, with q = ½(1 - R/C)^{-1} exceeding ½. The qualitative form Ṙ² = G(R) shows the closed model turns round at R = C while the flat and open models expand forever, the open one asymptotically linearly in t.
concepts: qualitative analysis of the Friedmann equation
key_moves: Substitute u² = R/C so the equation becomes separable with integrand u²/(1 - u²)^{1/2}.
Evaluate with u = sin θ, using sin²θ = (1 - cos 2θ)/2, to get C[arcsin (R/C)^{1/2} - (R/C)^{1/2}(1 - R/C)^{1/2}] = t, eq (25.19).
State the k = -1 analogue with sinh^{-1}, eq (25.20), as an exercise.
Differentiate implicitly to express H and q in terms of R for k = +1, eqs (25.21)-(25.22).
Use G(R) = C/R - k: G vanishes at R = C for k = +1 (recollapse); for k = -1, Ṙ² → 1 at large R so R ∼ t.

sections.title: Classification of Friedmann models
sections.summary: All the dust models are gathered in a single tabular figure organised by k (rows) and the sign of Λ (columns), with the k = +1, Λ > 0 cell split further. Open (k = -1, 0) models with Λ > 0 expand forever with an inflection ('kink'), with Λ = 0 expand forever (linearly or as t^{2/3}), and with Λ < 0 recollapse. For k = +1 a critical constant Λ_c = 4/(9C²) and radius R_c = 3C/2 separate Lemaître's model (Λ > Λ_c), the Einstein static model and its two asymptotic companions (Λ = Λ_c), and, for 0 < Λ < Λ_c, either an oscillating model or a bouncing model with no singularity; Λ ≤ 0 closed models oscillate. Cyclic repetition of oscillating models is mentioned.
key_moves: Organise models into Case I (k = -1), II (k = 0), III (k = +1) with sub-cases by sign or size of Λ: 3, 3 and 8 sub-cases.
Point out that all Λ < 0 models recollapse, calling them oscillating, and allow an indefinite sequence of cycles (Fig. 25.2).
Introduce the critical values Λ_c = 4/(9C²), R_c = 3C/2 for k = +1 (the double root of F(R) - 1).
Explain that the nearer Λ is to Λ_c from above, the longer the Lemaître model lingers near R_c.
At Λ = Λ_c distinguish three solutions by an integration constant: static, big bang approaching static, and static-in-the-past expanding to exponential (Eddington-Lemaître).
For 0 < Λ < Λ_c distinguish the oscillating branch from the time-symmetric bounce that stays away from R = 0.

sections.title: The Einstein static model and the de Sitter model
sections.summary: Setting R = a constant in the Robertson-Walker field equations shows that without Λ a static non-empty universe requires k = 1 and negative pressure, which is why Einstein added Λ; with Λ = 1/a² and k = 1 one gets dust of density 1/(4πa²), the Einstein static universe, now mainly useful as the canvas for Penrose diagrams. The de Sitter model (p = ρ = k = 0) has exponential scale factor, is the late-time limit of many models, and has a self-similar metric with no preferred time origin. A coordinate transformation turns it into a static form, so its apparent expansion is a coordinate effect.
concepts: static coordinates of de Sitter space
key_moves: Put R = a = constant and Λ = 0 in (24.52)-(24.53): 8πρ = 3k/a², 8πp = -k/a², so a non-trivial static model needs k = 1 and p < 0.
Restore Λ: 8πρ = 3k/a² - Λ, 8πp = Λ - k/a²; choose k = 1, Λ = 1/a² for a pressure-free static closed universe with ρ = 1/(4πa²).
Recall the historical sequence: galaxy recession led Einstein to abandon Λ, but Λ now returns as dark energy.
Set p = ρ = k = 0 to get Ṙ/R = (Λ/3)^{1/2}, R = exp[(Λ/3)^{1/2}t], and the flat-slicing line element with α = (3/Λ)^{1/2}.
Observe invariance under t → t + const with rescaled spatial coordinates, i.e. no natural origin of time.
Apply transformation (25.33) to reach the static form (25.34), exposing time independence of the metric components.

sections.title: Early epochs of the universe
sections.summary: Radiation should dominate gravity early on, so the equation of state 3p = ρ is imposed. With Λ = 0 the field equations reduce to R̈/R + Ṙ²/R² + k/R² = 0, giving R ∝ t^{1/2} at early times, faster than dust. The authors explain this as extra gravity from pressure, seen most clearly by imagining the collapse in reverse. The energy equation shows ρR⁴ is constant for radiation, and the Friedmann equation for radiation acquires a D/R² term.
concepts: scaling of density with scale factor
pressure as a source of gravity
key_moves: Impose 3p = ρ in (24.52)-(24.53) with Λ = 0 to obtain R̈/R + Ṙ²/R² + k/R² = 0.
Drop the k term at early times to get R ∼ t^{1/2}.
Compare with dust t^{2/3} and interpret via pressure contributing to gravity (argue with time-reversed collapse).
Use the energy equation (24.54) with p = 0 to get ρ ∝ R^{-3} and with p = ρ/3 to get ρR⁴ = constant.
Substitute into (24.52) to write Ṙ² = D/R² + ΛR²/3 - k with D = (8/3)πR⁴ρ.

sections.title: The steady-state theory
sections.summary: Summarises the 1948 Bondi-Gold-Hoyle theory, which buys simplicity and falsifiability at the cost of modifying energy conservation. From the perfect cosmological principle (the large-scale universe looks the same at all times) the observable spatial curvature kR^{-2} and Hubble parameter must be constant, forcing k = 0 and R = exp(t/T_0): the de Sitter line element. Light propagation then gives d_L proportional to the radial coordinate, 1 + z = exp[(t_0 - t_1)/T_0], an exactly linear Hubble law d_L = zT_0, and q = -1.
concepts: exact Hubble law in the steady-state model
key_moves: State the perfect cosmological principle and note it implies the ordinary cosmological principle, hence the Robertson-Walker form.
Argue that the 3-curvature ∝ kR^{-2} is observable, so constancy with growing R forces k = 0.
Argue that H = Ṙ/R is observable and hence constant, giving R = exp(t/T_0).
Integrate radial null rays: r = T_0(e^{-t/T_0} - e^{-t_0/T_0}) for rays arriving at r = 0 at t_0.
Combine d_L = r_1 e^{t_0/T_0} with 1 + z = R(t_0)/R(t_1) to get d_L = zT_0 exactly; compute q = -1.

sections.title: The event horizon of the de Sitter universe
sections.summary: Letting the reception time go to infinity in the past light cone equation gives the surface r = T_0 e^{-t/T_0}, beyond which the observer at r = 0 can never receive signals: an event horizon. A comoving particle at r = r_1 crosses it at t_1 = T_0 ln(T_0/r_1); signals it emits just before arrive ever later, with luminosity distance and redshift diverging, while the geodesic distance stays finite and the geodesic recession velocity tends to 1. Homogeneity makes this true for every comoving observer. An explorer can see beyond the observer's horizon but can never report back; the uniformly accelerated observer in Minkowski space gives a flat-space analogue.
concepts: reception time divergence at the horizon
key_moves: Take t_0 → ∞ in the past light cone (25.43) to obtain the horizon hypersurface (25.49).
Find the crossing time t_1 = T_0 ln(T_0/r_1) for a substratum particle P at r = r_1.
Integrate the null ray from (t, r_1) to r = 0 to get reception time τ = -T_0 ln(e^{-t/T_0} - e^{-t_1/T_0}).
Express d_L and z in terms of emission time and show both diverge as t → t_1, while P reaches the horizon in finite proper time.
Compute geodesic distance l = r_1 e^{t/T_0} (finite at P_1) and dl/dt = e^{(t - t_1)/T_0} → 1.
Introduce the curtain image and the explorer E who crosses the horizon at E_1; relate to the Minkowski horizon of a hyperbolic observer x² - t² = const.

sections.title: Particle and event horizons
sections.summary: Defines two kinds of horizon using conformal-diagram language. If scri-minus is spacelike, an observer's past light cone at any moment divides comoving particles into those already seen and not yet seen; the boundary is the particle horizon. If scri-minus is null (Minkowski) every particle is visible. If scri-plus is spacelike, the past light cone of the observer's endpoint on scri-plus is the future event horizon. If scri-plus is null, inertial observers have none but accelerated observers whose world-lines end on scri-plus do. Such horizons depend on the observer, in contrast to the absolute event horizons of black holes.
key_moves: Define the particle horizon of O at P from the intersection of P's past light cone with the family of particle world-lines when scri-minus is spacelike.
Contrast with null scri-minus, where the past cone reaches i^- and contains all particle histories.
Define the future event horizon as the past light cone of O's endpoint on a spacelike scri-plus.
For null scri-plus, show geodesic observers reach i^+ and have no event horizon while a uniformly accelerated observer ends on scri-plus and has one.
Stress observer dependence versus the absolute horizons of black holes.

sections.title: Lorentzian constant curvature space-times
sections.summary: Motivated by vacuum energy dominating late times, spacetimes with R_abcd = K(g_ac g_bd - g_ad g_bc) are studied. Contracting gives K = R/12 and G_ab = -3Kg_ab, so they are vacuum solutions with Λ = -3K, isotropic about every point. K = 0 is Minkowski space. De Sitter space is the hyperboloid -v̂² + ŵ² + x̂² + ŷ² + ẑ² = T_0² in a flat five-dimensional space with one timelike direction, topology R × S³, global metric dt̂² - T_0²cosh²(t̂/T_0)dΩ₃²; the steady-state (flat slicing) coordinates cover only the half ŵ + v̂ > 0. Anti-de Sitter space is the hyperboloid with two timelike embedding directions, metric T_0²[cosh²ρ d(t̂/T_0)² - dρ² - sinh²ρ dΩ²], whose periodic time is unwrapped to give topology R⁴.
concepts: hyperboloid embedding of de Sitter space
global coordinates of de Sitter space
flat slicing of de Sitter space
universal covering of anti-de Sitter space
key_moves: Argue that since dust dilutes as R^{-3} and radiation as R^{-4}, any Λ eventually dominates, so vacuum Λ solutions matter physically.
Contract the constant curvature condition twice to find K = R/12, then G_ab = -3Kg_ab, i.e. a vacuum solution with Λ = -3K.
Dispose of K = 0 as Minkowski space.
Embed de Sitter as a hyperboloid, parametrise with (t̂, χ, θ, φ) to get closed S³ slices contracting then re-expanding as cosh.
Introduce t = T_0 ln[(ŵ + v̂)/T_0] and scaled Cartesian coordinates to recover (25.31), and note they fail for ŵ + v̂ ≤ 0.
Embed AdS with two timelike directions, parametrise, observe 2π-periodic time and pass to the covering space.

sections.title: Conformal structure of Robertson-Walker space-times
sections.summary: Writing the Robertson-Walker metric with radial coordinate χ and conformal time dτ = dt/R shows ds² = R²(τ) ds̄² with ds̄² a static metric; for k = +1 that static metric is the Einstein static universe itself. For Λ = 0 the flat model maps to the upper half of the Minkowski compactification, the closed model to a band of the cylinder, and the open model to a smaller triangular region. Part of each boundary is now the initial singularity rather than infinity. Penrose diagrams follow: expanding models are triangles with a spacelike big bang at the bottom, the closed model is a rectangle with spacelike bang and crunch. Matter-filled Robertson-Walker universes are stated to be inextendible.
concepts: big bang singularity as a spacelike boundary
key_moves: Rewrite RW with χ, f(χ) = χ, sin χ, sinh χ for k = 0, +1, -1.
Define conformal time τ by dτ = dt/R to factor out R²(τ).
Recognise the k = +1 unphysical metric as the Einstein static cylinder (18.27) and map k = 0 onto the t' > 0 half of the Minkowski picture (Fig. 18.7).
Specify the k = -1 region by inequalities on t' ± r' and t' ≥ 0.
Draw shaded regions on the cylinder (Fig. 25.13) and the 2D Penrose diagrams (Figs 25.14, 25.15), noting that singular boundaries behave like any other boundary in the diagram.

sections.title: Conformal structure of de Sitter and anti-de Sitter space-time
sections.summary: The substitution t' = 2 arctan[exp(t̂/T_0)] - π/2 gives cosh(t̂/T_0) = 1/cos t' and makes de Sitter conformal to the band -π/2 < t' < π/2 of the Einstein static cylinder, a square Penrose diagram with spacelike scri-plus and scri-minus; the steady-state model is the half-triangle bounded by a null surface and so is geodesically incomplete to the past. For anti-de Sitter the radial substitution χ = 2 arctan(e^ρ) - π/2 gives cosh ρ = 1/cos χ, mapping AdS to half of the cylinder, 0 ≤ χ < π/2, whose boundary χ = π/2 is timelike. This timelike infinity underlies the AdS/CFT correspondence, mentioned as an active research topic.
concepts: Penrose diagram of de Sitter space
geodesic incompleteness of the steady-state model
timelike conformal boundary of anti-de Sitter space
key_moves: Define t' by an arctan of an exponential so that dt̂ = T_0 cosh(t̂/T_0) dt' and cosh(t̂/T_0) = sec t'.
Factor the global de Sitter metric as T_0² sec²t' times the Einstein static metric with t' restricted to (-π/2, π/2).
Identify the flat-slicing patch as half the square, bounded by a null surface through i^-, so the steady-state model is past-incomplete.
For AdS define χ from ρ the same way, getting T_0² sec²χ times the Einstein static metric with 0 ≤ χ ≤ π/2.
Conclude spatial slices are open hemispheres (topology R³), spacetime is R⁴, and infinity χ = π/2 is timelike.

sections.title: Our model of the universe
sections.summary: Summarises the domains of validity of the models. Homogeneity and isotropy hold only on large scales. Early on radiation dominates with R ∝ t^{1/2} and ρ ∝ R^{-4}; because radiation dilutes faster than dust (R^{-3}), matter eventually dominates with R ∝ t^{2/3}; in an ever-expanding universe any non-zero Λ, interpretable as vacuum energy with p = -ρ, eventually dominates, giving exponential growth towards de Sitter. An earlier exponential phase, inflation, driven by an inflaton field with T_ab ≈ V(φ)g_ab, precedes the radiation era. The sequence inflation → radiation → matter → vacuum is offered as the basic model, with real transitions being gradual and details deferred to the next chapter.
concepts: scaling of density with scale factor
key_moves: Recall observational support for large-scale homogeneity and isotropy and its breakdown on galactic scales.
Assign radiation-dominated, matter-dominated and vacuum-dominated laws R ∝ t^{1/2}, t^{2/3}, e^{αt}.
Use the different dilution rates to argue that the order of the eras is inevitable in an expanding universe.
Interpret Λ as a perfect fluid with p = -ρ (energy-momentum proportional to g_ab).
Add an early inflationary exponential stage driven by a slowly varying potential V(φ).
State the four-stage history and warn that the eras overlap in reality.

concepts.name: Friedmann equation for dust
concepts.definition: First-order equation for the scale factor of a homogeneous isotropic universe filled with pressure-free matter: Ṙ² = C/R + ΛR²/3 - k, with C > 0 fixed by the conserved mass, Λ the cosmological constant and k the curvature index.
concepts.how_introduced: Imported from Chapter 24 as the object to be solved; the chapter treats it as a non-linear ODE whose general solution is elliptic and attacks it by special cases and qualitative arguments.
concepts.notes: The book's (25.1) misprints the Λ term as ΛṘ/3; the correct term ΛR²/3 appears in (25.3) and (24.60).

concepts.name: scale factor
concepts.definition: The function R(t) multiplying the spatial part of the Robertson-Walker metric; ratios of R at two times give how much all comoving distances have grown.
concepts.how_introduced: Taken over from Chapter 24; every model in the chapter is described by the graph of R against cosmic time t.
concepts.notes: R is also used for the Ricci scalar in §25.9 (K = R/12); context distinguishes them.

concepts.name: Friedmann constant C
concepts.definition: Positive constant C = (8/3)πρR³ in the dust Friedmann equation, conserved because ρR³ is constant for dust; it sets the strength of gravitational attraction relative to curvature and Λ.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled with the requirement C > 0; it sets the characteristic scales Λ_c = 4/(9C²) and R_c = 3C/2 and the recollapse radius R = C for k = +1, Λ = 0.

concepts.name: cosmological constant
concepts.definition: Constant Λ in the field equations G_ab - Λg_ab = 8πT_ab (book's sign convention); in Friedmann's equation it contributes ΛR²/3, acting as repulsion for Λ > 0 and attraction for Λ < 0, and it can be reinterpreted as vacuum energy with p = -ρ.
concepts.how_introduced: Allowed any real value in the classification; its history (introduced by Einstein for a static universe, abandoned after Hubble, revived as dark energy) is retold in §25.4, and its late-time dominance motivates §25.9 and §25.12.

concepts.name: curvature index k
concepts.definition: Normalised constant k ∈ {-1, 0, +1} in the Robertson-Walker metric giving negatively curved, flat or positively curved spatial slices; the slice curvature scales as kR^{-2}.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to label the three rows of the classification; in §25.6 its observability (curvature ∝ kR^{-2}) is used to force k = 0 in the steady-state model.

concepts.name: big bang initial condition
concepts.definition: Choice of time origin so that the scale factor vanishes at t = 0; models satisfying it start from a singular state of zero scale factor.
concepts.how_introduced: Imposed as the lower limit when integrating each separable equation in §25.1-25.2.

concepts.name: Einstein-de Sitter model
concepts.definition: Spatially flat, pressure-free Friedmann model with Λ = 0, for which R = (9Ct²/4)^{1/3} ∝ t^{2/3}, H = 2/(3t) and q = 1/2 at all times.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by direct separation of Ṙ² = C/R; then shown to describe the early behaviour of every dust big bang model.

concepts.name: Hubble parameter
concepts.definition: Fractional expansion rate H = Ṙ/R of the scale factor; its reciprocal is a characteristic expansion time.
concepts.how_introduced: Computed from explicit solutions as a check (H = 2/(3t) for Einstein-de Sitter, formula in R for k = +1) and held constant in the steady-state argument.

concepts.name: deceleration parameter
concepts.definition: Dimensionless measure q = -RR̈/Ṙ² of whether the expansion is slowing (q > 0) or speeding up (q < 0).
concepts.how_introduced: Evaluated for Einstein-de Sitter (1/2), the closed dust model (greater than 1/2 and growing) and the steady-state model (-1).

concepts.name: qualitative analysis of the Friedmann equation
concepts.definition: Writing the Friedmann equation as Ṙ² = F(R) and inferring the history from F: R can only move where F ≥ 0, zeros of F are turning points, and the dominant term of F at small or large R gives power-law or exponential asymptotics.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced right after the exact k = 0 solutions as a cheaper route that generalises to all cases; repeated with G(R) = C/R - k for Λ = 0; it underpins the sketches of Fig. 25.1.
concepts.notes: Equivalent to one-dimensional particle motion in a potential; Exercise 25.7 draws the Newtonian analogy.

concepts.name: early-time universality of expansion
aliases: all big bang models start like Einstein-de Sitter
concepts.definition: Near R = 0 the matter term C/R dominates the curvature and Λ terms, so every dust big bang model grows as t^{2/3} initially regardless of k and Λ (t^{1/2} for radiation).
concepts.how_introduced: Argued by term dominance in (25.1) and integrated as in the Einstein-de Sitter case; revisited for radiation in §25.5 and in the summary §25.12.

concepts.name: late-time exponential expansion
concepts.definition: In any ever-expanding model with Λ > 0, the ΛR²/3 term eventually dominates and R grows like exp[(Λ/3)^{1/2}t], approaching the de Sitter model.
concepts.how_introduced: Found for k = 0 by dominance; §25.4 then observes that the Λ > 0 ever-expanding cases of every row (the kinked open and flat models, Lemaître's model, the Eddington-Lemaître model and the bounce) all approach it.

concepts.name: closed Friedmann model
concepts.definition: Positively curved dust model; with Λ = 0 it expands from a big bang to maximum scale factor R = C and recollapses, with the implicit solution C[arcsin(R/C)^{1/2} - (R/C)^{1/2}(1 - R/C)^{1/2}] = t.
concepts.how_introduced: Solved by the substitutions u² = R/C and u = sin θ; qualitatively from G(R) = C/R - 1 vanishing at R = C.
concepts.notes: Parametrically R = C sin²θ, t = C(θ - sin θ cos θ): a cycloid; maximum at t = πC/2, crunch at t = πC.

concepts.name: open Friedmann model
concepts.definition: Negatively curved dust model; with Λ = 0 it expands forever, starting as t^{2/3} and approaching R ≈ t since Ṙ² → 1 at large R.
concepts.how_introduced: Solution (25.20) stated as an exercise; asymptotics from G(R) = C/R + 1.

concepts.name: classification of Friedmann models
concepts.definition: Division of dust Friedmann models into 14 qualitatively distinct histories labelled by k (I: -1, II: 0, III: +1) and by the sign or size of Λ relative to the critical value Λ_c for k = +1.
concepts.how_introduced: Built by combining exact solutions and F(R) reasoning, then displayed as a grid of hand-drawn R(t) sketches with verbal descriptions of each sub-case.
prerequisites: qualitative analysis of the Friedmann equation
concepts.notes: Key lesson: with Λ ≠ 0 spatial curvature no longer decides fate (closed models can expand forever, open ones can recollapse).

concepts.name: critical cosmological constant
concepts.definition: For k = +1 dust models, Λ_c = 4/(9C²) is the value at which F(R) - 1 has a double root at R_c = 3C/2, allowing Ṙ = R̈ = 0 simultaneously; it separates ever-expanding from recollapsing or bouncing closed models.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated when enumerating Case III; Exercise 25.6 derives it via the rescaled variables x = R/R_c and λ = Λ/Λ_c.

concepts.name: Lemaître model
concepts.definition: Closed dust model with Λ slightly greater than Λ_c: a big bang, a long near-static coasting phase near R_c, then exponential expansion; the closer Λ is to Λ_c the longer the pause.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed as sub-case III(i) and sketched with a pronounced plateau.

concepts.name: Einstein static universe
concepts.definition: Static, closed (k = +1) dust universe with Λ = 1/a² and density ρ = 1/(4πa²), where cosmic repulsion exactly balances attraction; its line element dt'² - dr'² - sin²r' dΩ² on R × S³ is the canvas for conformal diagrams.
concepts.how_introduced: First as model III(iia) with R = R_c, then derived in §25.4 from the static field equations, which show that without Λ a static model would need negative pressure; reused in §25.10-25.11 as the conformal background.
concepts.notes: The book does not discuss that it is unstable to perturbations.

concepts.name: Eddington-Lemaître model
concepts.definition: Closed dust model with Λ = Λ_c that tends to the Einstein static state in the infinite past and expands to exponential growth in the future.
concepts.how_introduced: One of three solutions with Λ = Λ_c distinguished by an integration constant.

concepts.name: bouncing cosmological model
concepts.definition: Closed dust model with 0 < Λ < Λ_c that contracts from exponential size, reaches a positive minimum radius and re-expands symmetrically, never reaching R = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Second branch of sub-case III(iii), sketched as a U-shaped curve above the oscillating branch.

concepts.name: oscillating Friedmann model
concepts.definition: Model that expands from a big bang, halts and recollapses to a big crunch; all Λ < 0 models and closed models with Λ ≤ 0 or below Λ_c on the lower branch are of this type; a cyclic sequence of such arches is also contemplated.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in the classification; the indefinitely repeating version is sketched in Fig. 25.2.

concepts.name: big crunch
concepts.definition: Final state R → 0 of a recollapsing model, the time reverse of a big bang; on the Penrose diagram it is a spacelike boundary.
concepts.how_introduced: Named when Λ < 0 halts expansion; drawn as the top edge of the closed-model Penrose diagram.

concepts.name: inflection (coasting) phase in Friedmann models
concepts.definition: Interval in a Λ > 0 model where attraction and repulsion nearly balance, so R̈ changes sign from negative to positive and the growth rate dips before exponential expansion takes over.
concepts.how_introduced: Called a 'kink' in sub-cases I(i), II(i) and III(i).
concepts.notes: Inflection radius formula is our addition, derived from (25.1).

concepts.name: open and closed spatial topology
concepts.definition: Whether spatial sections are non-compact (k = 0, -1 in the simplest topology) or compact 3-spheres (k = +1).
concepts.how_introduced: Asserted at the head of each case in §25.3.
concepts.notes: Local curvature does not fix global topology; flat or hyperbolic slices can be compactified by identifications. The book uses the simplest topologies.

concepts.name: de Sitter model
concepts.definition: Empty (p = ρ = 0) spatially flat Robertson-Walker spacetime with Λ > 0 and scale factor R = exp[(Λ/3)^{1/2}t]; line element dt² - e^{2t/α}(dx² + dy² + dz²) with α = (3/Λ)^{1/2}.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the earliest expanding model (1917), derived from (24.52) with p = ρ = k = 0, identified as the late-time limit of many models, and later reinterpreted as the steady-state metric and as half of de Sitter space.

concepts.name: self-similarity of exponential expansion
concepts.definition: Invariance of the de Sitter flat-slicing metric under t → t + t_0 combined with rescaling spatial coordinates by e^{-t_0/α}; intrinsic measurements cannot identify a preferred epoch.
concepts.how_introduced: Pointed out when fixing the integration constant A = 1, and set as Exercise 25.8.
formulas: t \to t + t_0,\ x^i \to e^{-t_0/\alpha} x^i

concepts.name: static coordinates of de Sitter space
concepts.definition: Coordinates in which the de Sitter metric has time-independent components: g_tt = 1 - r²/α², with a coordinate horizon at r = α.
concepts.how_introduced: Reached by transformation (25.33) from the exponential form; used to show the expansion in (25.31) is an artefact of slicing. The reader is prompted to explain why the result is stationary.
concepts.notes: In spherical form this is (1 - r²/α²)dt² - dr²/(1 - r²/α²) - r²dΩ²; the book leaves that step to the reader.

concepts.name: radiation equation of state
concepts.definition: Pressure equals one third of energy density, as for a gas of photons or ultra-relativistic particles.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by radiation dominating gravity in early epochs; imposed on the Robertson-Walker field equations.
concepts.notes: The text twice writes p = 3ρ (in §25.5 and §25.12) where p = ρ/3 is meant.

concepts.name: radiation-dominated expansion
concepts.definition: Early-time behaviour R ∝ t^{1/2} of a universe whose gravity is dominated by radiation, faster initial growth than the t^{2/3} of dust.
concepts.how_introduced: From (25.36) with the k term neglected and from the D/R² term in (25.38); interpreted via pressure adding to gravity.

concepts.name: scaling of density with scale factor
concepts.definition: Energy conservation in an expanding RW universe gives ρ ∝ R^{-3} for pressure-free matter (number dilution) and ρ ∝ R^{-4} for radiation (dilution plus redshift); a cosmological constant keeps constant density.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived from the energy equation (24.54) for p = 0 and p = ρ/3; reused in §25.9 and §25.12 to argue the order of cosmic eras.

concepts.name: Friedmann equation for radiation
concepts.definition: Ṙ² = D/R² + ΛR²/3 - k with D = (8/3)πR⁴ρ constant, governing a radiation-filled Robertson-Walker universe.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by substituting ρ ∝ R^{-4} into (24.52); the book declines to classify its solutions.
prerequisites: scaling of density with scale factor
concepts.notes: Text says 'set C = (8/3)πD', which contradicts (25.39); it should be D = (8/3)πC with C = ρR⁴.

concepts.name: pressure as a source of gravity
concepts.definition: In general relativity pressure contributes to the gravitational field (the combination ρ + 3p drives deceleration), so a hot radiation-filled universe decelerates more strongly than dust.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as the physical reason radiation models expand as t^{1/2}; the authors suggest thinking of collapse in reverse, where more gravity means faster infall.
concepts.notes: The ρ + 3p formula is our addition; the book gives only the verbal argument.

concepts.name: steady-state theory
concepts.definition: 1948 cosmology in which the universe looks the same at all epochs; expansion is compensated by continuous creation of matter (violating standard energy conservation), and the metric is the exponential de Sitter form with Hubble time T_0.
concepts.how_introduced: Summarised in its original Bondi-Gold formulation, praised for making sharp predictions and hence being falsifiable, and noted as disfavoured by observation.

concepts.name: perfect cosmological principle
concepts.definition: The universe presents the same large-scale appearance not only from every place but at every time; it implies the ordinary cosmological principle plus stationarity of all observables.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as the founding assumption of the steady-state theory; later (§25.9) described geometrically as isotropy about every spacetime point.

concepts.name: stationarity
concepts.definition: Property that observable quantities do not change with time (for a metric: existence of coordinates with time-independent components).
concepts.how_introduced: Used twice: as the consequence of the perfect cosmological principle that forces k = 0 and constant H, and as the hidden property of the de Sitter metric revealed by (25.34).

concepts.name: exact Hubble law in the steady-state model
concepts.definition: In the steady-state (de Sitter) metric luminosity distance is exactly proportional to redshift at all distances, with proportionality constant the Hubble time.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by combining the null-ray solution, d_L = r_1 e^{t_0/T_0} and 1 + z = e^{(t_0 - t_1)/T_0}.

concepts.name: luminosity distance
concepts.definition: Distance inferred from observed flux of a source of known luminosity assuming the inverse-square law; in RW, d_L = r_1R(t_0) in the book's definition (24.72).
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 24 and evaluated in the steady-state and de Sitter horizon calculations.

concepts.name: cosmological redshift
concepts.definition: Fractional wavelength stretching of light between emission and reception, 1 + z = R(t_0)/R(t_1).
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from (24.66) and used to derive the exact Hubble law and to show infinite redshift at the de Sitter horizon.

concepts.name: cosmological event horizon
concepts.definition: Boundary of the set of events that an observer can ever receive signals from: the past light cone of the endpoint of the observer's world-line at future infinity; in de Sitter with comoving observer at r = 0 it is r = T_0 e^{-t/T_0}.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived as the t_0 → ∞ limit of the past light cone (25.48); then defined in general in §25.8 as the past light cone of O's endpoint on spacelike scri-plus.

concepts.name: reception time divergence at the horizon
concepts.definition: Signals emitted by a source just before it crosses an observer's event horizon arrive at later and later observer times, with reception time → ∞ as emission approaches the crossing event.
concepts.how_introduced: Computed explicitly from τ = -T_0 ln(e^{-t/T_0} - e^{-t_1/T_0}).

concepts.name: infinite redshift at a horizon
concepts.definition: As a source approaches an observer's event horizon both its luminosity distance and redshift grow without bound, although the source crosses in finite proper time and its geodesic distance stays finite.
concepts.how_introduced: Shown from (25.52)-(25.54) for a comoving particle in de Sitter.

concepts.name: geodesic recession velocity
concepts.definition: Rate of change with cosmic time of the proper (geodesic) distance l = R(t)r_1 between comoving observers; it can reach and exceed 1 without contradicting relativity because it is not a locally measured velocity.
concepts.how_introduced: Computed for de Sitter: dl/dt = e^{(t - t_1)/T_0} tends to the speed of light at the horizon.
concepts.notes: The printed (25.55) omits the division by T_0 in the exponent. The book does not discuss speeds beyond 1 for t > t_1.

concepts.name: observer dependence of event horizons
concepts.definition: Cosmological and acceleration horizons depend on the observer's world-line: moving elsewhere changes which events are hidden, unlike absolute black hole horizons.
concepts.how_introduced: Made vivid by the explorer who can see past O's horizon but never report, and restated in §25.8.

concepts.name: Rindler horizon
aliases: horizon of a uniformly accelerated observer
concepts.definition: In Minkowski space a uniformly accelerated observer on x² - t² = const has a null plane (x = t) beyond which emitted light can never catch up, an event horizon absent for inertial observers.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 3 (Fig. 3.8) as a flat-space analogue of the de Sitter horizon (Fig. 25.6), and used in §25.8 for the null scri-plus case.

concepts.name: particle horizon
concepts.definition: For an observer at event P, the boundary in the family of comoving particle world-lines between those whose past history lies inside P's past light cone (already observable) and those that do not; exists when scri-minus (the initial boundary) is spacelike.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined pictorially (Fig. 25.7) and contrasted with the null scri-minus case (Fig. 25.8) where every particle is visible.
concepts.notes: The integral formula is our addition; the book gives no quantitative expression.

concepts.name: conformal infinity (scri)
concepts.definition: Boundary added by conformal compactification: 𝒥⁻ where past-directed null (or all) curves originate, 𝒥⁺ where future-directed ones end; it can be null (Minkowski), spacelike (de Sitter, big bang or crunch in RW) or timelike (AdS).
concepts.how_introduced: Its causal character is used in §25.8 to predict horizons, then read off from the Penrose diagrams of §25.10-25.11.
concepts.notes: The reading copy OCR renders the script I as J.

concepts.name: absolute event horizon
concepts.definition: Event horizon defined by the global structure (boundary of the causal past of all of future null infinity), independent of any particular observer.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned only as a contrast to observer-dependent cosmological horizons.

concepts.name: constant curvature spacetime
concepts.definition: Spacetime whose Riemann tensor has the form R_abcd = K(g_ac g_bd - g_ad g_bc) with constant K; it is isotropic about every point, has K = R/12 in four dimensions and satisfies G_ab = -3Kg_ab.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the late-time dominance of Λ and by the perfect cosmological principle; generalises the constant curvature 3-spaces of §24.7-24.8 to Lorentzian signature.
concepts.notes: With the book's field equations (13.5) this gives Λ = -3K; combined with (24.52) de Sitter then has K = -1/α² < 0, whereas the text labels K > 0 as de Sitter (see gaps).

concepts.name: Einstein space
concepts.definition: Spacetime whose Ricci tensor is proportional to the metric, R_ab = λg_ab; equivalently a vacuum solution with a cosmological constant.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled: isotropy about every point implies an Einstein space, guaranteed by constant curvature.

concepts.name: de Sitter space
concepts.definition: The complete maximally symmetric vacuum spacetime with positive cosmological constant: a one-sheeted hyperboloid of radius T_0 in flat five-dimensional Minkowski space, topology R × S³, with global metric dt̂² - T_0²cosh²(t̂/T_0)dΩ₃².
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as Case II of constant curvature spacetimes by embedding, then related to the flat (steady-state) coordinates, and finally compactified to a square Penrose diagram.
formulas: -\hat v^2 + \hat w^2 + \hat x^2 + \hat y^2 + \hat z^2 = T_0^2
ds^2 = d\hat t^2 - T_0^2\cosh^2(\hat t/T_0)\,[d\chi^2 + \sin^2\chi\, d\Omega^2]

concepts.name: hyperboloid embedding of de Sitter space
concepts.definition: Realising a constant-curvature spacetime as a quadric surface in a flat higher-dimensional space whose induced metric is the desired one, so the symmetry group is visible as the rotation/boost group of the embedding space.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to 'most easily visualise' de Sitter and anti-de Sitter, with explicit parametrisations (25.61) and (25.66) and pictures (Figs 25.11, 25.12).

concepts.name: global coordinates of de Sitter space
concepts.definition: Coordinates covering the whole de Sitter hyperboloid with spatial 3-sphere slices whose radius T_0 cosh(t̂/T_0) contracts to a minimum then expands; comoving observers are geodesics normal to these slices.
concepts.how_introduced: Given by parametrisation (25.61); covers the hyperboloid for all real t̂ apart from polar coordinate degeneracies.
formulas: \hat v = T_0\sinh(\hat t/T_0),\ \hat w = T_0\cosh(\hat t/T_0)\cos\chi,\ \dots

concepts.name: flat slicing of de Sitter space
concepts.definition: Coordinates t = T_0 ln[(ŵ + v̂)/T_0], x^i = T_0 x̂^i/(ŵ + v̂) in which de Sitter has flat spatial slices and exponential scale factor; they cover only the half of the hyperboloid with ŵ + v̂ > 0, bounded by a null surface.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced to connect the embedding to (25.31)/(25.41), revealing that the steady-state model is only half of de Sitter space.
formulas: t = T_0\ln[(\hat w+\hat v)/T_0],\ x = T_0\hat x/(\hat w+\hat v)

concepts.name: anti-de Sitter space
concepts.definition: Maximally symmetric vacuum spacetime with negative cosmological constant: the hyperboloid -û² - v̂² + x̂² + ŷ² + ẑ² = -T_0² in a flat 5-space with two timelike directions, with metric T_0²[cosh²ρ d(t̂/T_0)² - dρ² - sinh²ρ dΩ²]; after unwrapping the periodic time it has topology R⁴ and a timelike conformal boundary.
concepts.how_introduced: Case III of constant curvature spacetimes, set up in parallel with de Sitter but with the sign changes emphasised; compactified onto half the Einstein static cylinder.
prerequisites: hyperboloid embedding of de Sitter space
formulas: ds^2 = T_0^2[\cosh^2\rho\, d(\hat t/T_0)^2 - d\rho^2 - \sinh^2\rho\, d\Omega^2]
concepts.notes: The printed (25.64) drops the square on û.

concepts.name: universal covering of anti-de Sitter space
concepts.definition: Replacing the embedded AdS hyperboloid, whose time coordinate is 2π-periodic (closed timelike curves), by the spacetime with the same metric and t̂ ranging over all reals.
concepts.how_introduced: Justified as removing an artefact of the embedding construction.

concepts.name: vacuum domination
concepts.definition: Late stage of an ever-expanding universe in which the constant-density Λ term outgrows matter (R^{-3}) and radiation (R^{-4}) terms, so R ∝ e^{αt} with α = (Λ/3)^{1/2}.
concepts.how_introduced: Argued in §25.9 as motivation for studying de Sitter, named in §25.12.
prerequisites: scaling of density with scale factor

concepts.name: conformal time
concepts.definition: Time coordinate τ with dτ = dt/R(t), in which the Robertson-Walker metric factors as R²(τ) times a static metric, so radial light rays move at 45°.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced to map RW spacetimes onto regions of the Einstein static cylinder.
concepts.notes: In §25.7 τ denotes a reception time instead.

concepts.name: conformal compactification
aliases: conformal mapping onto the Einstein static universe
concepts.definition: Multiplying a metric by a positive factor that brings infinity (or singular boundaries) to finite coordinate values, producing an 'unphysical' metric with the same light cones whose region can be drawn in full.
concepts.how_introduced: Carried over from Chapter 18 and applied first to RW, then de Sitter and AdS, each time identifying the static metric with the Einstein static line element (18.27).

concepts.name: Penrose diagram of Robertson-Walker models
concepts.definition: Two-dimensional causal diagram of a Friedmann model with angular directions suppressed: a triangle with spacelike big bang base for k = 0, -1 (Λ = 0) and a rectangle with spacelike bang and crunch for k = +1.
concepts.how_introduced: Drawn after shading the corresponding cylinder regions in Fig. 25.13; the authors note the singular boundary changes little in how the diagrams are drawn.
prerequisites: big bang singularity as a spacelike boundary

concepts.name: big bang singularity as a spacelike boundary
concepts.definition: In Friedmann models the R = 0 singularity forms a spacelike surface of the conformal diagram, so different comoving observers originate from causally disconnected points of it (the origin of particle horizons).
concepts.how_introduced: Read off the Penrose diagrams in §25.10.

concepts.name: inextendibility of Robertson-Walker models
concepts.definition: Matter-filled Robertson-Walker spacetimes cannot be embedded as proper subsets of larger spacetimes; the singular boundaries are genuine edges.
concepts.how_introduced: Asserted without proof at the end of §25.10.

concepts.name: Penrose diagram of de Sitter space
concepts.definition: Square conformal diagram of global de Sitter space occupying -π/2 < t' < π/2, 0 ≤ χ ≤ π on the Einstein static cylinder, with spacelike 𝒥⁻ and 𝒥⁺.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained from t' = 2 arctan[exp(t̂/T_0)] - π/2 and drawn alongside the steady-state half.

concepts.name: geodesic incompleteness of the steady-state model
aliases: past incompleteness of flat de Sitter patch
concepts.definition: The steady-state spacetime ends on a null boundary in the past, so some geodesics reach it at finite affine parameter even though comoving observers exist for infinite past time.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off from the Penrose diagram Fig. 25.17(b) and described as an aesthetic defect.
prerequisites: flat slicing of de Sitter space
Penrose diagram of de Sitter space

concepts.name: timelike conformal boundary of anti-de Sitter space
concepts.definition: Compactified AdS occupies 0 ≤ χ < π/2 of the Einstein static cylinder; its infinity χ = π/2 is a timelike hypersurface that light can reach and return from in finite coordinate time.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived with χ = 2 arctan(e^ρ) - π/2 and pictured in Fig. 25.18.

concepts.name: AdS/CFT correspondence
concepts.definition: Conjectured equivalence between a quantum gravity (string) theory in anti-de Sitter space and a conformal field theory living on its timelike boundary.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the reason AdS matters despite not being a cosmological model; declared beyond the book's scope.
prerequisites: timelike conformal boundary of anti-de Sitter space

concepts.name: cosmic history sequence
concepts.definition: Standard qualitative history: early inflationary exponential expansion, then radiation domination (t^{1/2}), matter domination (t^{2/3}), and eventual vacuum domination approaching de Sitter, with gradual transitions.
concepts.how_introduced: Assembled in the closing section from the density scalings and the special solutions of the chapter.
prerequisites: scaling of density with scale factor

concepts.name: matter domination
concepts.definition: Epoch when pressure-free matter dominates the Friedmann equation, R ∝ t^{2/3} at small R, which necessarily follows radiation domination because radiation dilutes faster.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in the summary §25.12.
prerequisites: scaling of density with scale factor

concepts.name: vacuum energy
concepts.definition: Energy density of empty space (for example quantum zero-point energy) behaving as a perfect fluid with p = -ρ, whose energy-momentum tensor is proportional to the metric and is therefore equivalent to a cosmological constant.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered in passing as a possible physical origin of a small Λ.
concepts.notes: The book writes T_ab = Λg_ab, dropping the 1/(8π) required by (13.5).

concepts.name: inflation
concepts.definition: Hypothesised very early phase of near-exponential expansion driven by a scalar field φ whose potential energy V(φ) makes T_ab ≈ V(φ)g_ab, acting as a temporary cosmological constant; its decay starts the radiation era.
concepts.how_introduced: Sketched in two sentences in §25.12 with detail deferred to the next chapter.

concepts.name: dark energy
concepts.definition: Name for whatever component with strongly negative pressure drives the present accelerated expansion; a cosmological constant is the simplest version.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned when explaining that Λ has returned to cosmology (§25.4); the closing section also attaches the name to the inflaton's matter content.
concepts.notes: Standard usage reserves 'dark energy' for the late-time component; applying it to the inflaton is unusual.

key_equations.name: Friedmann's equation (dust)
key_equations.meaning: Master equation of the chapter: expansion rate squared balances matter attraction, Λ repulsion and curvature. The printed (25.1) has ΛṘ in place of ΛR²; the corrected form is given here.
key_equations.symbols: R scale factor; C = (8/3)πρR³ > 0; Λ cosmological constant; k curvature index

key_equations.name: Parameter ranges
key_equations.meaning: Domain of the classification.

key_equations.name: Flat-space Friedmann equation
key_equations.meaning: Special case k = 0.

key_equations.name: Substitution for k = 0, Λ > 0
key_equations.meaning: Change of variable that turns (25.3) into an integrable form.
Transformed equation; completing the square and u + 1 = cosh w integrates it.

key_equations.name: Flat model with positive Λ
key_equations.meaning: Big bang model that starts as t^{2/3} and grows exponentially at late times.
Substitution for Λ < 0.

key_equations.name: Flat model with negative Λ
key_equations.meaning: Recollapsing flat model; maximum R³ = 3C/(-Λ) at half period.

key_equations.name: Einstein-de Sitter model
key_equations.meaning: Flat dust model with Λ = 0; R ∝ t^{2/3}.

key_equations.name: Hubble parameter of Einstein-de Sitter
key_equations.meaning: Age of an Einstein-de Sitter universe is 2/(3H).

key_equations.name: Deceleration parameter of Einstein-de Sitter
key_equations.meaning: Constant deceleration parameter.

key_equations.name: Early-time behaviour
key_equations.meaning: Every dust big bang model starts like Einstein-de Sitter.

key_equations.name: Qualitative form
key_equations.meaning: Behaviour of R read from the sign and zeros of F.

key_equations.name: Maximum radius for Λ < 0
key_equations.meaning: Zero of F where expansion halts. The book calls it a local minimum; it is the maximum of R(t).

key_equations.name: Late-time behaviour for Λ > 0
key_equations.meaning: Exponential (de Sitter-like) growth at late times.

key_equations.name: Friedmann equation with Λ = 0
key_equations.meaning: Starting point of §25.2. The inline text's 'Ṙ = C/R - 1' should read Ṙ² = C/R - 1.
Substitution for k = ±1; followed by u = sin θ (k = +1).

key_equations.name: Separated integral for k = +1
key_equations.meaning: Evaluated with u = sin θ to θ - sin θ cos θ.

key_equations.name: Closed dust model (Λ = 0)
key_equations.meaning: Implicit expansion-recollapse history; equivalently R = C sin²θ, t = C(θ - sin θ cos θ).

key_equations.name: Open dust model (Λ = 0)
key_equations.meaning: Ever-expanding hyperbolic model, asymptotically R ≈ t.

key_equations.name: Hubble parameter, closed model
key_equations.meaning: Vanishes at maximum expansion R = C.

key_equations.name: Deceleration parameter, closed model
key_equations.meaning: Always above 1/2, diverging at turnaround.
Qualitative form for Λ = 0: G vanishes at R = C only when k = +1.

key_equations.name: Critical cosmological constant
key_equations.meaning: Separates closed models that expand forever from those that recollapse or bounce.

key_equations.name: Critical scale factor
key_equations.meaning: Radius of the Einstein static model for given C.

key_equations.name: Static RW equations without Λ
key_equations.meaning: A static non-empty universe with Λ = 0 needs k = 1 and negative pressure.

key_equations.name: Static RW equations with Λ
key_equations.meaning: With k = 1, Λ = 1/a² gives dust of density 1/(4πa²): the Einstein static universe.
Friedmann equation for empty flat space with Λ.

key_equations.name: de Sitter model
key_equations.meaning: Exponential expansion; integration constant set to 1.

key_equations.name: de Sitter line element (flat slicing)
key_equations.meaning: Standard exponential form.
de Sitter radius / Hubble time.

key_equations.name: Transformation to static coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Removes the explicit time dependence.

key_equations.name: Static form of de Sitter
key_equations.latex: ds^2 = \left[1 - \alpha^{-2}r^2\right]dt^2 - dx^2 - dy^2 - dz^2 - \frac{\alpha^{-2}(x\,dx + y\,dy + z\,dz)^2}{1 - \alpha^{-2}r^2},\quad r^2 = x^2+y^2+z^2
key_equations.meaning: Manifestly stationary: the expansion in (25.31) is a coordinate effect.

key_equations.name: Radiation equation of state
key_equations.meaning: Ultra-relativistic matter.
Radiation-filled RW with Λ = 0; neglecting k gives R ∼ t^{1/2}.

key_equations.name: Radiation energy conservation
key_equations.meaning: Radiation dilutes as R^{-4}. The text says p = 3ρ here; it should be p = ρ/3.

key_equations.name: Friedmann equation for radiation
key_equations.meaning: Radiation analogue of (25.1).
Constant of the radiation Friedmann equation (so D = (8/3)π × const of (25.37), not the reverse stated in the text).

key_equations.name: Steady-state scale factor
key_equations.meaning: Constant Hubble parameter 1/T_0 with k = 0.

key_equations.name: Steady-state line element
key_equations.meaning: Same as de Sitter in spherical coordinates (the printed bracket placement is slightly off).

key_equations.name: Radial null rays
key_equations.meaning: Light propagation in the steady-state metric.

key_equations.name: Past light cone of (t_0, r = 0)
key_equations.meaning: Incoming ray reaching the origin at t_0.
Luminosity distance proportional to coordinate r.
Redshift in terms of coordinate distance.

key_equations.name: Exact Hubble law
key_equations.meaning: Linear distance-redshift relation at all z in the steady-state model.
Accelerating expansion in the steady-state model.

key_equations.name: Past light cone (restated)
key_equations.meaning: Starting point for the horizon; the printed version erroneously has t_0 in both exponents.

key_equations.name: de Sitter event horizon
key_equations.meaning: Limit t_0 → ∞ of the past light cone: the observer at r = 0 never receives signals from outside.

key_equations.name: Horizon crossing time
key_equations.meaning: When comoving particle at r_1 crosses O's horizon.

key_equations.name: Reception time
key_equations.meaning: Arrival time at O of a signal sent by P at t < t_1; diverges as t → t_1.
key_equations.symbols: τ here is reception time, not conformal time

key_equations.meaning: Luminosity distance O assigns to P; diverges at the horizon.
Redshift diverges with d_L.

key_equations.name: Geodesic distance
key_equations.meaning: Proper distance at time t; finite at crossing.

key_equations.name: Geodesic recession velocity
key_equations.meaning: Tends to 1 (speed of light) at the horizon. The printed exponent omits the division by T_0.

key_equations.name: Uniformly accelerated world-line
key_equations.meaning: Minkowski observer with an event horizon (Fig. 25.6).

key_equations.name: Constant curvature condition
key_equations.meaning: Maximally symmetric spacetime.
Double trace in four dimensions.
Vacuum solution with Λ = -3K under G_ab - Λg_ab = 8πT_ab.

key_equations.name: de Sitter hyperboloid
key_equations.latex: -\hat v^2 + \hat w^2 + \hat x^2 + \hat y^2 + \hat z^2 = T_0^2
key_equations.meaning: Embedding surface, topology R × S³.

key_equations.name: Five-dimensional flat metric
key_equations.latex: ds^2 = d\hat v^2 - d\hat w^2 - d\hat x^2 - d\hat y^2 - d\hat z^2
key_equations.meaning: Minkowski metric in five dimensions (one timelike direction).

key_equations.name: Global parametrisation
key_equations.latex: \hat v = T_0\sinh\tfrac{\hat t}{T_0},\ \hat w = T_0\cosh\tfrac{\hat t}{T_0}\cos\chi,\ \hat x = T_0\cosh\tfrac{\hat t}{T_0}\sin\chi\cos\theta,\ \hat y = T_0\cosh\tfrac{\hat t}{T_0}\sin\chi\sin\theta\cos\phi,\ \hat z = T_0\cosh\tfrac{\hat t}{T_0}\sin\chi\sin\theta\sin\phi
key_equations.meaning: Covers the full hyperboloid.

key_equations.name: Global de Sitter metric
key_equations.meaning: Closed slicing: 3-spheres contract then expand.

key_equations.name: Flat slicing coordinates
key_equations.latex: t = T_0\ln\left[(\hat w + \hat v)/T_0\right],\ x = T_0\hat x/(\hat w+\hat v),\ y = T_0\hat y/(\hat w+\hat v),\ z = T_0\hat z/(\hat w+\hat v)
key_equations.meaning: Recover (25.31) with α = T_0 on the half ŵ + v̂ > 0.

key_equations.name: Anti-de Sitter hyperboloid
key_equations.meaning: Embedding surface for AdS (printed with -û for -û²).

key_equations.latex: ds^2 = d\hat u^2 + d\hat v^2 - d\hat x^2 - d\hat y^2 - d\hat z^2
key_equations.meaning: Flat 5-metric with two timelike directions.

key_equations.name: AdS parametrisation
key_equations.latex: \hat u = T_0\sin\tfrac{\hat t}{T_0}\cosh\rho,\ \hat v = T_0\cos\tfrac{\hat t}{T_0}\cosh\rho,\ \hat x = T_0\sinh\rho\cos\theta,\ \hat y = T_0\sinh\rho\sin\theta\cos\phi,\ \hat z = T_0\sinh\rho\sin\theta\sin\phi
key_equations.meaning: Time is periodic on the hyperboloid.

key_equations.name: Global AdS metric
key_equations.meaning: Static global AdS (a stray 'n' precedes ds² in print).

key_equations.name: RW metric with χ
key_equations.meaning: Form used for conformal analysis.
Radial functions; the text's range 0 to 2π for k = +1 should be 0 to π.

key_equations.name: Conformal time
key_equations.meaning: Removes R from the time part.

key_equations.name: Conformal factorisation
key_equations.latex: ds^2 = R^2(\tau)\,d\bar s^2,\qquad d\bar s^2 = d\tau^2 - d\chi^2 - f^2(\chi)(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2)
key_equations.meaning: RW is conformal to a static spacetime; for k = +1 the Einstein static universe.

key_equations.name: Conformal region for k = -1
key_equations.meaning: Portion of the Einstein static cylinder occupied by the open dust model (stated without proof).

key_equations.name: de Sitter conformal time
key_equations.meaning: Compactifies global de Sitter time.

key_equations.name: Conformal de Sitter
key_equations.latex: ds^2 = T_0^2\cosh^2(\hat t/T_0)\,d\bar s^2 = \frac{T_0^2}{\cos^2 t'}\,d\bar s^2,\quad d\bar s^2 = dt'^2 - d\chi^2 - \sin^2\chi\,d\Omega^2
key_equations.meaning: de Sitter is conformal to a finite band of the Einstein static cylinder (printed cosh²(t'/T_0) should be cosh²(t̂/T_0)).

key_equations.name: AdS radial compactification
key_equations.meaning: Brings ρ = ∞ to χ = π/2.
Relation used to factor the AdS metric.

key_equations.name: Conformal anti-de Sitter
key_equations.meaning: AdS is conformal to half the Einstein static cylinder with timelike boundary χ = π/2.

key_equations.name: Vacuum-dominated growth
key_equations.meaning: Late-time behaviour of any ever-expanding universe with Λ > 0.

key_equations.name: Inflaton energy-momentum
key_equations.meaning: A slowly rolling scalar field mimics a cosmological constant.

key_equations.name: Rescaled Friedmann equations (Exercise 25.6)
key_equations.latex: \ddot R = \frac{2}{9C}\left(-x^{-2} + \lambda x\right),\qquad \dot R^2 = \tfrac13\left(2x^{-1} + \lambda x^2 - 3k\right),\qquad x = R/R_c,\ \lambda = \Lambda/\Lambda_c
key_equations.meaning: Dimensionless form exposing the critical point x = λ = k = 1.

key_equations.name: Newtonian channel analogue (Exercise 25.7)
key_equations.meaning: Radial Newtonian motion whose energy equation mirrors Friedmann's with Λ = 0.

figures.label: Fig. 25.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: Table of sketches showing every qualitative type of dust Friedmann model.
figures.visual_description: A ruled table. Rows are labelled I (k = -1), II (k = 0), III (k = +1); columns are Λ > 0, Λ = 0, Λ < 0. Each cell holds a small R-versus-t sketch with a lower-case Roman numeral. Rows I and II, Λ > 0: a curve rising steeply from the origin, flattening through an inflection, then turning upward. Row I, Λ = 0: a concave curve becoming nearly straight. Row II, Λ = 0: a concave curve labelled Einstein-de Sitter. Both Λ < 0 cells: a symmetric arch from R = 0 back to R = 0. Row III's Λ > 0 cell is split into three sub-columns. Λ > Λ_c (i): a curve with a long flat plateau, labelled Lemaître. Λ = Λ_c (ii): a horizontal line labelled Einstein (iia), a curve rising from the origin that levels off below the line (iib), and a curve lifting off above the line and growing (iic, Eddington-Lemaître). Λ_c > Λ > 0 (iii): a U-shaped curve that never reaches R = 0 (iiib) above an arch (iiia). Row III, Λ = 0 (iv) and Λ < 0 (v): arches.
figures.what_it_teaches: The whole model space at a glance. Fate depends on both k and Λ; the (k, Λ) plane has a special structure near Λ_c for closed models; all big bang curves leave the origin the same way.

redesign.idea: Live Friedmann explorer: a (Ω_Λ-like Λ/Λ_c, k) parameter plane beside a plot of R(t) computed by numerically integrating Ṙ² = C/R + ΛR²/3 - k. The fourteen book cases are marked as regions, lines and points in the plane.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags a point in the (λ = Λ/Λ_c, k) plane or picks a book label (e.g. III(iiib)). The R(t) curve updates, along with the potential-like plot of F(R) - k with the 'energy' level, the turning points and the H, q readouts. A toggle overlays all fourteen canonical curves.

figures.label: Fig. 25.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: A model that recollapses and restarts repeatedly.
figures.visual_description: Axes R (vertical) and t (horizontal). Two complete identical arches each start and end at R = 0, touching the t axis in cusps; a third arch begins at the right and is cut off, with the label 'etc.'.
figures.what_it_teaches: Recollapsing models could in principle be followed by further cycles, giving an indefinitely oscillating universe.

redesign.idea: Animated cyclic universe: an arch-by-arch R(t) trace with a shrinking and growing sphere icon, plus a note on whether the book's dust equations actually permit passage through R = 0.
redesign.interaction: Play/pause and a slider for Λ < 0 changes the period and peak height via (25.7). A switch shows the cusp at each bounce, to prompt discussion of what physics would be needed there.

figures.label: Fig. 25.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: The exponential scale factor of the de Sitter model.
figures.visual_description: Axes R (vertical, through the middle) and t (horizontal). A single smooth exponential curve is close to the t axis at far left for negative t, crosses the R axis at a positive value, and rises steeply to the right. It never reaches R = 0.
figures.what_it_teaches: de Sitter expansion has no beginning, is defined for all t, and looks the same at every epoch up to a shift: the self-similarity point.

redesign.idea: Self-similarity zoom: an exponential curve that the learner can pan along; after rescaling the vertical axis the view is indistinguishable at every epoch.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags a window along t; an 'auto-rescale' toggle renormalises R so the curve inside the window stays identical, while a power-law curve for comparison visibly changes shape.

figures.caption_paraphrase: No caption; a decorative note-taking grid printed in the page margin.
figures.visual_description: A narrow block of empty rectangular cells in two columns and about seven rows, drawn with thin black lines and holding no text or symbols. It is the printed margin grid that appears down the edge of many pages in this edition, not a physics figure.
figures.what_it_teaches: Nothing about physics; it is layout decoration.

redesign.idea: No redesign needed.
redesign.interaction: None.

figures.label: Fig. 25.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: A comoving observer's event horizon in the de Sitter universe.
figures.visual_description: Spacetime diagram with time upward. A vertical line in the centre is observer O at r = 0, and a vertical line to its right is particle P at r = r_1. Two curved boundaries, one on each side, are far apart at the bottom and approach O's line towards the top; the regions outside them are hatched. A label 'Event horizon of O' has leader lines to both boundaries. P's world-line crosses the right boundary at a dot marked P_1 (t_1, r_1). Below P_1 a cross marks an emission event (t, r_1). A dotted arrowed curve runs from it up and to the left to a dot on O's line near the top, marked (τ, 0) and labelled 'Signal from P to O'.
figures.what_it_teaches: The horizon shrinks in comoving coordinate r, so every comoving particle eventually crosses it. Signals sent just below P_1 arrive at O ever later, and nothing sent after P_1 ever arrives.
concepts: reception time divergence at the horizon

redesign.idea: Horizon crossing simulator: the (t, r) diagram with the horizon curve r = T_0 e^{-t/T_0}, a draggable source world-line, and a stream of signals whose arrival times, redshifts and d_L are plotted live.
redesign.interaction: Learner sets r_1 and scrubs the emission time t. The null ray to O redraws, a side panel plots τ(t), z(t) and dl/dt from (25.51)-(25.55), and all diverge or reach 1 as t → t_1. A second tab shows the same in proper distance, where the horizon is the fixed distance T_0.

figures.label: Fig. 25.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: An explorer sent out by O can see beyond O's horizon but cannot report back.
figures.visual_description: Same style of diagram as Fig. 25.4: a vertical line 'World-line of O' in the centre and hatched regions beyond two curved horizon boundaries labelled 'Event horizon of O'. A second world-line, 'World-line of E', branches off O's line low down, runs diagonally up to the right, then turns upward and crosses the right-hand horizon boundary at a point marked 'Event E_1'. Dotted arrowed null lines run up and to the left from E's world-line towards O's line before E_1. Beyond E_1, inside the hatched region, a dotted arrowed line heads left but does not reach O.
figures.what_it_teaches: Event horizons belong to observers: E's own horizon differs from O's, but crossing O's horizon severs communication with O for ever.

redesign.idea: Two-observer horizon game: launch an explorer with chosen velocity profile, see both observers' horizons drawn simultaneously, and watch which of E's reports reach O.
redesign.interaction: Learner draws or parametrises E's trajectory; reports (null rays) are emitted at regular intervals, coloured green if they reach O and red if not; E's own horizon and the region E can see beyond O's horizon are shaded.

figures.label: Fig. 25.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: Minkowski space-time event horizon of a uniformly accelerated observer.
figures.visual_description: t (vertical) and x (horizontal) axes. A hyperbola in the right-hand wedge is labelled 'World-line of uniformly accelerated observer P', with an arrow pointing upward. A solid 45° line through the origin rises to the upper right. Everything above and left of it is hatched and labelled 'P's event horizon'. A solid line runs down to the right from the origin. On the hyperbola below the x axis sits the point P_0. Dashed lines leave P_0 down to the left and down to the right, marked 'Past light cone of event P_0'.
figures.what_it_teaches: Horizons are not special to curved spacetime: in flat space an accelerated observer has one and an inertial observer does not, which makes the cosmological horizon less mysterious.

redesign.idea: Rindler vs inertial toggle: a Minkowski diagram where the learner sets proper acceleration; the hyperbola, its asymptote horizon and the unreachable region update, and emitted light pulses from events in the hatched region visibly never meet the world-line.
redesign.interaction: Slider for acceleration a (hyperbola x² - t² = 1/a²); click anywhere to fire a light pulse and see whether it intersects the world-line; switch to a = 0 to see the horizon disappear.

figures.label: Fig. 25.8
figures.caption_paraphrase: When past null infinity is null, an observer's past light cone contains every particle.
figures.visual_description: A V-shaped pair of straight lines meeting at a bottom vertex labelled i⁻; the left arm is labelled 𝒥⁻ (the OCR reads it as J). Several gently wavy particle world-lines fan upward from i⁻. One is labelled 'O's world-line' and carries the point P. Straight lines from P down to i⁻ form the past light cone, labelled 'Past light cone of O at P'.
figures.what_it_teaches: With null 𝒥⁻ (as in Minkowski space) all particle histories start at i⁻ inside every past light cone, so there is no particle horizon.

redesign.idea: Paired with Fig. 25.7 in a single toggle: switch the bottom boundary between null (V shape) and spacelike (flat) and watch the set of visible particle world-lines change.
redesign.interaction: Learner moves P up O's world-line; visible particle world-lines light up; the boundary type toggle demonstrates when a particle horizon exists.

figures.label: Fig. 25.7
figures.caption_paraphrase: Particle horizon of an observer when past null infinity is spacelike.
figures.visual_description: A gently undulating horizontal curve along the bottom is labelled 𝒥⁻. About eight wiggly particle world-lines rise from it. The central one, 'O's world-line', carries a dot P. Two straight lines from P down to the bottom curve form 'Past light cone of O at P'. Regions to the left and right, away from the cone's footprint, are hatched. Labels: 'Particle world-lines' (left group), 'Particle horizon for O at P' (the world-line at the edge of what can be seen), 'Particles not yet observed by O at P' (the hatched ones on the right).
figures.what_it_teaches: A spacelike initial boundary means O's past cone cuts off a finite set of particles; the boundary world-line is the particle horizon, which moves outward as P rises.
concepts: big bang singularity as a spacelike boundary

redesign.idea: Particle horizon growth: conformal diagram of an Einstein-de Sitter universe with comoving world-lines; as the learner advances cosmic time the past cone widens and newly visible galaxies light up, with the comoving particle horizon distance plotted against t.
redesign.interaction: Time slider moves P; hovering a galaxy shows the redshift at which it first became visible; option to switch to a model with inflation that pushes 𝒥⁻ down and removes horizons.

figures.label: Fig. 25.9
figures.caption_paraphrase: Future event horizon when both past and future infinity are spacelike.
figures.visual_description: A horizontal band bounded below by a wavy line marked 𝒥⁻ and above by one marked 𝒥⁺. Several roughly vertical world-lines cross the band. O's world-line meets 𝒥⁺ at the apex of a triangle whose sloping sides come down to the lower boundary. The region outside the triangle is filled with horizontal hatching, labelled 'Event which will never be seen by O'. The triangle's edge is labelled 'O's future event horizon'.
figures.what_it_teaches: The future event horizon is the past light cone of O's final point on a spacelike 𝒥⁺; events outside it never influence O.

redesign.idea: Horizon finder on a de Sitter Penrose square: learner drags an observer's world-line endpoint along 𝒥⁺, and the event horizon and invisible region redraw.
redesign.interaction: Drag endpoint; click events to test whether they will ever be seen; compare two observers' horizons with different colours.

figures.label: Fig. 25.10
figures.caption_paraphrase: When future null infinity is null, only non-geodesic observers ending on it have event horizons.
figures.visual_description: Upper part of a Minkowski Penrose diagram: two straight lines meet at an apex labelled i⁺; the left line is labelled 𝒥⁺. A wavy curve 'O's geodesic world-line' ends at i⁺. A second curve 'Ō's non-geodesic world-line' bends right and ends on the right-hand boundary line below the apex. A dashed 45° line parallel to that boundary runs up from the lower left to Ō's endpoint, labelled 'Ō's future event horizon'.
figures.what_it_teaches: In Minkowski space only observers whose world-lines end on 𝒥⁺ (uniformly accelerated ones) have a horizon; inertial observers see everything eventually.

redesign.idea: Compactified Minkowski diamond with draggable world-lines; the tool computes where each world-line hits the boundary and draws the horizon if it ends on 𝒥⁺.
redesign.interaction: Learner chooses inertial, uniformly accelerated or custom acceleration profile; horizon appears only when the endpoint is on 𝒥⁺.

figures.label: Fig. 25.11
figures.caption_paraphrase: de Sitter space as a hyperboloid in five-dimensional Minkowski space.
