figures.visual_description: A waisted hyperboloid of one sheet drawn in perspective, narrowest in the middle and flaring at top and bottom. Horizontal ellipses are labelled 'Surfaces t̂ = constant: constant positive curvature S³', and the narrowest one is t̂ = 0. Vertical meridian curves are labelled 'Geodesic normals'. Two meridians at the top carry the labels χ = 0 and χ = π.
figures.what_it_teaches: Global de Sitter: closed spatial slices shrink to a minimum radius T_0 and re-expand, comoving observers are the meridians, and the topology is R × S³.
concepts: global coordinates of de Sitter space
hyperboloid embedding of de Sitter space

redesign.idea: 3D de Sitter hyperboloid (two spatial dimensions suppressed) with switchable slicings: global circles, flat (steady-state) slices and static patches, each drawn on the same surface.
redesign.interaction: Learner rotates the hyperboloid, chooses a slicing, scrubs its time parameter to move the slice, and toggles the null surface ŵ + v̂ = 0 to see which half the flat coordinates cover; boosts in the embedding space can be applied to show homogeneity.

figures.label: Fig. 25.12
figures.caption_paraphrase: de Sitter space in the flat (t, x, y, z) coordinates covers only part of the hyperboloid.
figures.visual_description: The same waisted hyperboloid with a dashed ellipse at its base. Many straight lines run diagonally across its surface and converge towards a point at lower right, labelled 'Null surface t̂ = -∞' and 'Geodesic normals'. Curved lines near the top are labelled 'Surface of constant time t'.
figures.what_it_teaches: The steady-state coordinates slice de Sitter by flat sections whose normals diverge from a point in the infinite past; a null surface bounds the covered region, so only half the spacetime is described.
concepts: flat slicing of de Sitter space

redesign.idea: Included in the Fig. 25.11 3D tool as the flat-slicing mode, with the uncovered half ghosted.
redesign.interaction: Same as Fig. 25.11; additionally, a geodesic launched into the ghosted region shows it leaving the steady-state patch at finite affine parameter.

figures.label: Fig. 25.13 (k = 0 panel)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Region of the Einstein static cylinder conformal to the flat Λ = 0 Robertson-Walker model.
figures.visual_description: A vertical cylinder with generators labelled χ = 0, χ = ½π (front and back) and χ = π, and dashed horizontal ellipses at t' = 0 and t' = π. A shaded region starts at the t' = 0 ellipse and rises to a peak on the χ = 0 side, sloping down towards the far side, with cross-hatching on the lower part and single hatching on the sloping upper part. Label k = 0 underneath. The inventory tags this image 'Fig. 25.13'; it is the first of three panels.
figures.what_it_teaches: The flat model occupies the future half of the compactified Minkowski region: bottom edge is the big bang, sloping top edge is future null infinity.

redesign.idea: Einstein static cylinder painter: one 3D cylinder with a model selector (k = 0, +1, -1, de Sitter, AdS, steady state) that shades the conformal region, with a side-by-side 2D unrolled Penrose diagram.
redesign.interaction: Learner selects a model and scrubs cosmic time; a constant-t slice glows on both the cylinder and the flat diagram; light rays can be launched to show 45° propagation and horizons.

figures.label: Fig. 25.13 (k = +1 panel)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Region of the Einstein static cylinder conformal to the closed Λ = 0 model.
figures.visual_description: A cylinder with two dashed horizontal ellipses. The band between them is uniformly cross-hatched all the way round. Vertical generator lines, label k = +1 below. The inventory mislabels this image as Fig. 25.14; it is the middle panel of Fig. 25.13.
figures.what_it_teaches: The closed model is a finite-height band of the cylinder bounded by spacelike big bang and big crunch surfaces.

redesign.idea: Model option in the cylinder painter above, with the band height computed from ∫dt/R (2π for dust).
redesign.interaction: Switching between dust and radiation filling changes the band height (2π vs π), and a photon launched at the bang shows how far round the 3-sphere it gets.

figures.label: Fig. 25.13 (k = -1 panel)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Region of the Einstein static cylinder conformal to the open Λ = 0 model.
figures.visual_description: A cylinder with dashed horizontal ellipses and vertical generators. Near the bottom ellipse a small hatched hump rises to a peak on the left side and tapers along the ellipse to the right. It is much lower and narrower than the k = 0 region. Label k = -1 below. The inventory mislabels this image as Fig. 25.15; it is the third panel of Fig. 25.13.
figures.what_it_teaches: The open model maps to a smaller triangular region (t' ± r' bounded by π/2), still with a spacelike big bang base and null future boundary.

redesign.idea: Model option in the cylinder painter.
redesign.interaction: As above.

figures.label: Fig. 25.14
figures.caption_paraphrase: Penrose diagram of the ever-expanding Λ = 0 models (k = 0 and -1).
figures.visual_description: A right triangle. The vertical left edge is χ = 0, the horizontal bottom edge is labelled '𝒥⁻ (t = 0) Big bang', and the hypotenuse slopes down from the apex i⁺ at top left to the bottom right, labelled 𝒥⁺. Curved lines bowing upward span the triangle ('Surfaces t = constant'). Straight lines fan from i⁺ down to the base ('World-lines of fundamental particles').
figures.what_it_teaches: Big bang is a spacelike lower boundary; comoving observers converge to i⁺; future infinity is null. The geometry of horizons can be read directly.
concepts: big bang singularity as a spacelike boundary

redesign.idea: Interactive Penrose triangle for Einstein-de Sitter with exact conformal coordinates, clickable events showing their past light cones and particle horizons.
redesign.interaction: Learner clicks events; past cone and the set of galaxies inside it highlight; slider converts between cosmic time labels and conformal coordinates.

figures.label: Fig. 25.15
figures.caption_paraphrase: Penrose diagram of the closed Λ = 0 model.
figures.visual_description: A rectangle, wider than it is tall, filled with a fine square grid. The top edge is labelled '𝒥⁺ (τ = π) Big crunch', the bottom edge '𝒥⁻ (τ = 0) Big bang', the left edge χ = 0 and the right edge χ = π. Horizontal grid lines are labelled 'Surfaces t = constant' and vertical ones 'World-lines of fundamental particles'.
figures.what_it_teaches: Both bang and crunch are spacelike. Every comoving observer runs from bottom to top, and the diagram's proportions set how much of the universe light can cross in its lifetime.

redesign.idea: Closed universe light-crossing demo: rectangle with correct proportions (width π, height 2π for dust), photon emitted at the bang travelling at 45° to show it makes exactly one circuit before the crunch.
redesign.interaction: Learner picks matter content (dust/radiation) and emission event; the photon path redraws and wraps at χ = π; the book's drawn proportions can be toggled for comparison.

figures.label: Fig. 25.16
figures.caption_paraphrase: Region of the Einstein static cylinder conformal to de Sitter space.
figures.visual_description: A cylinder with generators labelled r' = 0 and r' = π. Horizontal ellipses are labelled from top to bottom 𝒥⁺ (t' = ½π), t' = constant, t' = 0 and 𝒥⁻ (t' = -½π), the last drawn dashed. The band between 𝒥⁻ and 𝒥⁺ is shaded. A curved line crosses it diagonally from lower left to upper right and divides it into a cross-hatched part and a single-hatched part.
figures.what_it_teaches: Global de Sitter is conformal to a band of height π on the cylinder with spacelike boundaries at both ends; the diagonal hints at the null surface bounding the steady-state half.
concepts: Penrose diagram of de Sitter space
flat slicing of de Sitter space

redesign.idea: de Sitter option in the cylinder painter, with the flat-slicing half highlighted.
redesign.interaction: Toggle flat-slicing overlay; scrub t̂ to watch its image t' approach ±π/2.

figures.label: Fig. 25.17
figures.caption_paraphrase: Penrose diagrams of (a) de Sitter space and (b) the steady-state model.
figures.visual_description: (a) A square filled with a grid. Horizontal lines are 'Surface t̂ = constant' and vertical lines 'Time lines'. The top edge is 𝒥⁺ and the bottom edge 𝒥⁻; tick labels χ = 0 (lower left side) and χ = π (upper right side). (b) The same square with only the upper-left triangle drawn in. A diagonal runs from i⁻ at bottom left to i⁰ at top right and is labelled 𝒥⁻. Curved lines fanning from i⁻ are the time lines, curved arcs are surfaces of constant t̂ (constant t in the flat slicing), and the top edge is 𝒥⁺.
figures.what_it_teaches: Global de Sitter has spacelike past and future infinity. The steady-state universe is exactly half of it, with a null past boundary, so it is geodesically incomplete in the past despite being eternal for comoving observers.
concepts: Penrose diagram of de Sitter space
geodesic incompleteness of the steady-state model
flat slicing of de Sitter space

redesign.idea: Half-and-whole de Sitter: square Penrose diagram with a draggable diagonal mask; geodesics shot backwards from inside the steady-state half exit through the null boundary at finite affine parameter.
redesign.interaction: Learner fires timelike or null geodesics with a chosen direction; a counter shows affine parameter to the boundary; toggling the mask shows the full de Sitter continuation.

figures.label: Fig. 25.18
figures.caption_paraphrase: Conformal anti-de Sitter space-time.
figures.visual_description: Two panels. Left: a tall rectangle whose left edge is labelled z = 0, with a vertical dashed line and a horizontal dashed midline. Two straight diagonals run from the left corners to the midpoint of the right edge, enclosing a triangular wedge. Inside, above the midline, 'z > 0, t > 0'; below it, 'z > 0, t < 0'. Arrows mark the upper diagonal 'z = +∞, t = +∞' and the lower one 'z = +∞, t = -∞'. Right: a cylinder with ellipses at top, middle and bottom and a dashed vertical axis with dots at the top and bottom centres. Dashed and dotted curves run from the bottom rim up to the right-hand side at mid-height, and from there up to the top rim.
figures.what_it_teaches: AdS is conformal to half of the Einstein static cylinder, with a timelike boundary (χ = π/2) that light reaches in finite coordinate time and returns from. The left panel shows a region (labelled with z, t coordinates the text never defines, i.e. a Poincaré-type patch) bounded by null surfaces.
concepts: timelike conformal boundary of anti-de Sitter space

redesign.idea: AdS 'box' demo: half-cylinder (or 2D strip) where the learner fires massive particles that oscillate back to the centre and light rays that hit the boundary and reflect, with an optional overlay of the Poincaré patch wedge.

worked_examples.problem: Solve the flat dust Friedmann equation with positive Λ subject to a big bang start.
worked_examples.method: Set u = 2ΛR³/(3C) to get u̇² = 3Λ(2u + u²). Take the positive root and write 2u + u² = (u + 1)² - 1. Substitute u + 1 = cosh w, so the integral becomes ∫dw, and invert.
worked_examples.key_insight: Choosing the variable ∝ R³ makes both terms of F(R) quadratic in u, so the integral becomes standard.
worked_examples.result: R³ = (3C/2Λ)[cosh((3Λ)^{1/2}t) - 1]; the Λ < 0 analogue has 1 - cos.

worked_examples.problem: Find R(t), H and q for the flat, Λ = 0 dust model.
worked_examples.method: Separate Ṙ² = C/R as R^{1/2}dR = C^{1/2}dt, integrate from R = 0 at t = 0, then differentiate.
worked_examples.key_insight: The simplest big bang model already has universal early-time behaviour and constant q.

worked_examples.problem: Solve the closed (k = +1), Λ = 0 dust model and find H and q.
worked_examples.method: Substitute u² = R/C to get a separable equation with integrand 2u²/(1 - u²)^{1/2}. Put u = sin θ, use the double-angle identity, and express the result back in R. Differentiate implicitly for H and q.
worked_examples.key_insight: The trigonometric substitution exposes the cycloid: expansion to R = C and symmetric recollapse.

worked_examples.problem: Can the Robertson-Walker field equations admit a static universe filled with ordinary matter?
worked_examples.method: Set R = a constant in (24.52)-(24.53), first with Λ = 0 and then with Λ free, and impose ρ ≥ 0 and p = 0.
worked_examples.key_insight: Without Λ a static universe needs negative pressure; with Λ = 1/a² and k = 1 dust can sit still. This is the logic that led Einstein to Λ.
worked_examples.result: Λ = 0: 8πρ = 3k/a², 8πp = -k/a² (needs k = 1, p < 0). With Λ: k = 1, Λ = 1/a², ρ = 1/(4πa²), p = 0.

worked_examples.problem: Show that the exponentially expanding de Sitter metric is actually stationary.
worked_examples.method: Apply the transformation (25.33): t̄ = t - (α/2)ln[1 - α^{-2}r²e^{2t/α}], x̄^i = x^i e^{t/α}. Substitute into (25.31) and drop bars.
worked_examples.key_insight: Physical coordinates x̄ = e^{t/α}x absorb the expansion; the logarithmic time shift removes the cross terms, leaving metric components that do not depend on t.
worked_examples.result: ds² = (1 - r²/α²)dt² - dx² - dy² - dz² - α^{-2}(x dx + y dy + z dz)²/(1 - r²/α²), eq (25.34).
concepts: static coordinates of de Sitter space

worked_examples.problem: How do density and scale factor behave in a radiation-filled universe?
worked_examples.method: Insert 3p = ρ into the field equations with Λ = 0 to get R̈/R + Ṙ²/R² + k/R² = 0 and drop k at early times. Put p = ρ/3 in the energy equation (24.54) to get d(ρR⁴)/dt = 0, then substitute into (24.52).
worked_examples.key_insight: Radiation loses energy to redshift as well as dilution, and its pressure adds to gravity, so the early expansion law changes from t^{2/3} to t^{1/2}.
worked_examples.result: ρ ∝ R^{-4}, R ∼ t^{1/2}, Ṙ² = D/R² + ΛR²/3 - k with D = (8/3)πR⁴ρ.
concepts: scaling of density with scale factor

worked_examples.problem: Derive the steady-state metric from the perfect cosmological principle and deduce its Hubble law and deceleration parameter.
worked_examples.method: Observable 3-curvature kR^{-2} must be constant, so k = 0. Observable H must be constant, so R = e^{t/T_0}. Integrate radial null rays to get r(t), use d_L = r_1R(t_0) and 1 + z = R(t_0)/R(t_1), eliminate r_1.
worked_examples.key_insight: Demanding that observables, not coordinates, be time-independent pins down the geometry uniquely without any field equations.
worked_examples.result: ds² = dt² - e^{2t/T_0}[dr² + r²dΩ²], d_L = zT_0 exactly, q = -1.
concepts: exact Hubble law in the steady-state model

worked_examples.problem: For a comoving observer at r = 0 in de Sitter space, find the event horizon and describe what is seen of a comoving particle at r = r_1.
worked_examples.method: Take t_0 → ∞ in the past light cone to get r = T_0e^{-t/T_0}; solve for the crossing time t_1. Integrate a null ray from (t, r_1) to r = 0 for the reception time τ. Evaluate d_L = r_1e^{τ/T_0}, z = d_L/T_0, proper distance l = r_1e^{t/T_0} and its time derivative.
worked_examples.key_insight: Everything O observes diverges (arrival time, redshift, apparent distance) while the particle itself crosses at finite proper time and finite proper distance, where its geodesic recession speed equals light speed.
concepts: reception time divergence at the horizon

worked_examples.problem: Find the scalar curvature and Einstein tensor of a four-dimensional constant curvature spacetime.
worked_examples.method: Contract R_abcd = K(g_ac g_bd - g_ad g_bc) on a and c to get R_bd = 3Kg_bd, contract again for R = 12K, and form G_ab = R_ab - ½Rg_ab.
worked_examples.key_insight: Maximal symmetry automatically makes the spacetime a vacuum solution with a cosmological constant, so the constant-curvature classification is also a classification of Λ-vacua.
worked_examples.result: K = R/12, G_ab = -3Kg_ab, hence Λ = -3K with G_ab - Λg_ab = 0.

worked_examples.problem: Obtain global and flat-slicing coordinates on the de Sitter hyperboloid and the global metric of anti-de Sitter space.
worked_examples.method: Parametrise the quadric (25.59) with hyperbolic and spherical functions, check the constraint, and pull back the 5D metric to get (25.62). Define t = T_0 ln[(ŵ + v̂)/T_0] and x^i = T_0x̂^i/(ŵ + v̂) to get (25.31). Repeat with two timelike directions for AdS, (25.64)-(25.67).
worked_examples.key_insight: Embedding makes the maximal symmetry and the global topology visible, and shows that coordinate patches can cover only part of the manifold.
worked_examples.result: ds² = dt̂² - T_0²cosh²(t̂/T_0)dΩ₃² (all of de Sitter); flat coordinates only where ŵ + v̂ > 0; AdS: T_0²[cosh²ρ d(t̂/T_0)² - dρ² - sinh²ρ dΩ²] with t̂ unwrapped.
concepts: hyperboloid embedding of de Sitter space
global coordinates of de Sitter space
flat slicing of de Sitter space

worked_examples.problem: Construct the conformal diagrams of de Sitter and anti-de Sitter space.
worked_examples.method: For de Sitter set t' = 2arctan(e^{t̂/T_0}) - π/2 so that dt̂ = T_0 cosh(t̂/T_0)dt' and cosh(t̂/T_0) = sec t'; factor the metric as T_0² sec²t' times the Einstein static metric. For AdS apply the same trick to the radial coordinate, χ = 2arctan(e^ρ) - π/2, obtaining T_0² sec²χ times the Einstein static metric.
worked_examples.key_insight: The same 'double arctan of an exponential' (the Gudermannian function) compactifies an infinite hyperbolic range into a finite angular range; whether it acts on time or radius decides whether infinity is spacelike (dS) or timelike (AdS).
worked_examples.result: de Sitter: band -π/2 < t' < π/2 of the cylinder (square Penrose diagram, steady-state = half). AdS: 0 ≤ χ < π/2 for all t̂, timelike boundary at χ = π/2, topology R⁴.
concepts: Penrose diagram of de Sitter space
timelike conformal boundary of anti-de Sitter space

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: An event horizon is a curtain that hides what lies behind it; an explorer can pull the curtain aside, but only by leaving home for ever.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Used to convey both that information beyond the horizon is inaccessible to O and that those events are nonetheless real and observable to others at the cost of never returning.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: A curtain is a physical object at a place; the horizon is a null surface defined by O's entire future, not a barrier that anyone passing it would notice locally.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Animate a translucent curtain attached to the horizon surface in the (t, r) diagram that re-forms around E's position when the viewpoint switches from O to E.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Friedmann's equation read as a particle's energy equation: Ṙ² plays kinetic energy and -F(R) a potential, so turning points are where 'kinetic energy' vanishes.
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: qualitative analysis of the Friedmann equation
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Implicit in the F(R) and G(R) reasoning and made explicit in Exercise 25.7, where a particle falling in a straight channel toward a mass obeys ẋ² = 2GM/x - 2GM/x_1 and its escape or return mirrors open and closed models.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The 'energy' constant is -k, quantised to three values by normalisation. Λ gives a potential with no Newtonian counterpart in the simple channel model, and the analogy says nothing about spatial geometry.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Potential-well view: plot V(R) = -C/R - ΛR²/6 with a horizontal line at -k/2 and a ball rolling on it, synchronised with the R(t) plot.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: An exponential curve is self-similar: zooming to any portion and rescaling looks the same, so no moment along it is special.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Explains why de Sitter's time origin is conventional and prepares for the perfect cosmological principle.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Self-similarity of R(t) is a statement about the metric's symmetry; it does not by itself show the full spacetime is time-independent, which needs the static coordinates.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Run a collapse backwards in time: more gravity means faster collapse, so its time reverse is faster expansion from the singularity.
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: pressure as a source of gravity
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Used to make sense of the claim that radiation, with pressure, expands faster near the big bang than dust.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: 'Faster' needs care: at equal density radiation decelerates more, and the model reaches R = 0 more quickly when run backwards; comparing t^{1/2} with t^{2/3} directly depends on normalisation.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Split-screen reversed-time movie of dust and radiation collapses starting from the same R and Ṙ.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The uniformly accelerated observer in Minkowski space as a flat-space model for a cosmological horizon.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Shows that horizons arise from an observer's world-line relative to the causal structure rather than from curvature, then used to classify horizons by the nature of 𝒥⁺.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The Rindler horizon disappears if the observer stops accelerating; the de Sitter horizon exists for every geodesic comoving observer.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Side-by-side diagrams: Rindler hyperbola in Minkowski and a comoving observer in de Sitter (static patch), with matched horizon shading.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Visualising a curved spacetime as a surface (hyperboloid) sitting inside a flat higher-dimensional space.
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: hyperboloid embedding of de Sitter space
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Makes the global topology (cylinder R × S³), the contracting-then-expanding 3-spheres, and the partial coverage of flat coordinates visible at a glance.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The embedding space has indefinite signature, so Euclidean intuitions about distances on the drawn surface are misleading; the picture suppresses two or three dimensions.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: 3D rotatable hyperboloid with light cones drawn tangent to the surface to counter Euclidean intuition.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The Einstein static cylinder as a common stage on which every model becomes a shaded region.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Different cosmologies are compared by the shape of their region (band, triangle, half-cylinder), which directly reveals spacelike, null or timelike infinity.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Conformal maps preserve light cones but not distances or time intervals; the size of a region is not physically meaningful.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Cylinder painter with a model gallery.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Because the de Sitter metric contains e^{2t/α}, de Sitter space is intrinsically evolving.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Transforming to (25.34) gives time-independent components; the apparent expansion reflects the choice of comoving slicing. Comoving observers still separate, but the geometry is stationary.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Metrics written in comoving coordinates make any time dependence look physical.
concepts: static coordinates of de Sitter space

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Pressure pushes outward, so a radiation-filled universe should resist collapse and expand more gently than dust.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In general relativity pressure is a source of gravity, adding to the attraction, which is why radiation models behave as t^{1/2} near the singularity.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Everyday pressure pushes on walls; a homogeneous universe has no pressure gradients, and only the gravitating effect remains.
concepts: pressure as a source of gravity

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Closed universes always recollapse and open or flat universes always expand for ever.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: That link holds only for Λ = 0. With Λ > Λ_c a closed model expands for ever, and with Λ < 0 every model, including open ones, recollapses.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Many introductory treatments set Λ = 0 and equate geometry with destiny.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Event horizons exist only around black holes and are the same for everyone.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Cosmological and acceleration horizons depend on the observer's world-line; black hole horizons are the special absolute (observer-independent) kind.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Horizons are usually first met in black-hole contexts.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A galaxy crossing our cosmological horizon suddenly vanishes at some finite time we could observe.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Its light arrives ever later and ever more redshifted; we never see the crossing itself, though the galaxy passes the horizon in finite proper time.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: People picture the horizon like the edge of a field of view that objects step behind.
concepts: reception time divergence at the horizon

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Events beyond an observer's horizon can be ignored as physically meaningless.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: They are real: an explorer can see them and the observer's own horizon moves if the observer moves; only communication back is impossible.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Operationalist instinct that the unobservable does not exist.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A recession velocity reaching the speed of light violates relativity.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The geodesic recession velocity dl/dt is a rate of change of proper distance along a cosmic-time slice, not a velocity measured locally against light; it reaches 1 at the horizon without contradiction.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Special relativity is remembered as 'nothing can exceed c' without the qualifier 'locally'.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The big bang happened at a point in space.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In the Penrose diagrams the initial singularity is a spacelike surface: every comoving world-line starts on it, at different places.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Popular images of an explosion from a centre.
concepts: big bang singularity as a spacelike boundary

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A coordinate system that covers all of an observer's world-lines covers the whole spacetime.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The flat (steady-state) coordinates cover all comoving histories from t = -∞ yet only half of de Sitter space; geodesics leave the patch through a null boundary.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Coordinate time running from -∞ to +∞ sounds complete.
concepts: flat slicing of de Sitter space
geodesic incompleteness of the steady-state model

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: An eternal steady-state universe with no beginning is automatically complete.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Its Penrose diagram shows a null past boundary: some geodesics end at finite affine parameter, so it is past-incomplete.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: No big bang singularity suggests nothing is missing.
concepts: geodesic incompleteness of the steady-state model

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The periodic time in the AdS embedding means time is physically cyclic there.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The periodicity is an artefact of the embedding; one takes the covering space with t̂ over all reals, topology R⁴.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The formulas in (25.66) are manifestly periodic.
concepts: universal covering of anti-de Sitter space

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The Einstein static universe is a viable static cosmos once Λ is tuned.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It requires exact fine-tuning (Λ = Λ_c and R = R_c with Ṙ = R̈ = 0) and any perturbation sends it toward the Eddington-Lemaître or the collapsing branch; it is also contradicted by observed expansion.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The algebra gives a perfectly valid solution, and the book presents it as balanced.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Cosmic eras are cleanly separated, with radiation absent in the matter era and so on.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: All components coexist; each era is defined by which term dominates the Friedmann equation, and transitions are gradual.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Textbook tables list eras with sharp boundaries.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Spatial curvature k = +1 or 0 or -1 fixes whether space is finite.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Local geometry does not fix global topology; flat or hyperbolic spaces can be compact after identifications. The book's 'open/closed topology' assumes the simplest topologies.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The book states topology directly from k.

thought_experiments.name: Watching a comoving galaxy slip over the de Sitter horizon
thought_experiments.setup: Observer O at r = 0 monitors substratum particle P at r_1, receiving its signals and measuring their redshift and apparent distance.
thought_experiments.lesson: O's received signals take unboundedly long, with redshift and luminosity distance diverging, while P crosses the horizon at finite proper time; the recession speed reaches light speed there.

thought_experiments.name: The explorer who draws the curtain
thought_experiments.setup: O sends explorer E outward with instructions to report everything; E crosses O's horizon at event E_1.
thought_experiments.lesson: E can learn about events hidden from O but can never send that knowledge back; horizons are observer-relative and knowledge beyond them is available only one way.

thought_experiments.name: The uniformly accelerated observer in flat spacetime
thought_experiments.setup: An observer on x² - t² = const in Minkowski space and light emitted from events in the region t > x.
thought_experiments.lesson: Such light never reaches the observer, so a horizon exists without curvature; inertial observers have none.

thought_experiments.name: Particle in a straight channel toward a fixed mass
thought_experiments.setup: A test mass moves along a line under Newtonian attraction from a fixed mass at the origin, starting outward with some speed (Exercise 25.7).
thought_experiments.lesson: Its energy equation has the same form as Friedmann's with Λ = 0: returning, marginal and escaping motions correspond to closed, flat and open models.
concepts: qualitative analysis of the Friedmann equation
thought_experiments.app_idea: Side-by-side channel particle and universe radius with a shared energy slider.

thought_experiments.name: Reversing a collapse to understand radiation expansion
thought_experiments.setup: Imagine a radiation-filled and a dust-filled universe collapsing, then run the film backwards.
thought_experiments.lesson: Stronger gravity (with pressure) gives faster collapse; the reversed film is a faster initial expansion.
concepts: pressure as a source of gravity

historical_notes.event: Believing the universe static and homogeneous, Einstein found the field equations required negative pressure for a static closed universe and added the cosmological constant, obtaining the Einstein static universe.
historical_notes.significance: Origin of Λ; the static model survives today as the conformal backdrop for Penrose diagrams.

historical_notes.event: Observed that distant galaxies recede, showing the universe expands.
historical_notes.significance: Led Einstein to drop Λ and accept expanding models.

historical_notes.event: Found the empty exponentially expanding solution with Λ, the earliest expanding cosmological model.
historical_notes.significance: Became the late-time attractor of Λ > 0 models, the steady-state metric, and a prototype of inflation.

historical_notes.event: Closed models with Λ near the critical value (Lemaître's coasting model, the Eddington-Lemaître model emerging from the static state) are named after them.
historical_notes.significance: Early explorations of Λ-dominated histories; the book only uses the names as labels.

historical_notes.event: Proposed the steady-state theory based on the perfect cosmological principle with continuous matter creation.
historical_notes.significance: A sharply falsifiable rival to big bang cosmology, now considered mainly historical because observations disagree with it.

historical_notes.event: The cosmological constant returned to cosmology in the form of dark energy.
historical_notes.significance: Justifies keeping Λ throughout the classification.

historical_notes.event: Gave a systematic treatment of the solutions of Friedmann's equation in all cases.
historical_notes.significance: Cited as the complete reference the chapter does not reproduce.

historical_notes.event: The AdS/CFT correspondence links quantum gravity in anti-de Sitter space to conformal field theory on its boundary.
historical_notes.significance: Explains the modern interest in a spacetime that is not a realistic cosmology.

applications_and_observations.topic: Galaxy recession and abandonment of the static universe
applications_and_observations.details: Recession of distant galaxies measured by Slipher and Hubble showed expansion, ending the static Einstein model as a cosmology.

applications_and_observations.topic: Age of an Einstein-de Sitter universe
applications_and_observations.details: From H = 2/(3t), the age is two-thirds of the Hubble time. Our own estimate, not in the text: with H_0 ≈ 70 km/s/Mpc (Hubble time ≈ 14.0 Gyr) this gives about 9.3 Gyr, younger than the oldest stars. This is one historical motivation for Λ, taken up in Chapter 26.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: t_0 = 2/(3H_0) ≈ 9.3 Gyr for H_0 = 70 km/s/Mpc (our estimate)

applications_and_observations.topic: Steady-state predictions: exact Hubble law and q = -1
applications_and_observations.details: The theory predicts d_L = zT_0 at all redshifts and q = -1, making it easy to test; the text says it conflicts with much present-day observation (details such as the microwave background and evolving radio-source counts are not given here).

applications_and_observations.topic: Size of our cosmological event horizon
applications_and_observations.details: If the universe approaches de Sitter with the observed Λ, the asymptotic horizon distance is α = (3/Λ)^{1/2}. Our own estimate: Λ ≈ 1.1 × 10^{-52} m^{-2} gives α ≈ 1.6 × 10^{26} m ≈ 17 billion light years.

Because ρ_rad ∝ R^{-4} and ρ_matter ∝ R^{-3}, radiation must dominate early and matter later. Our own addition from standard ΛCDM values: equality occurs at redshift about 3400, and matter-Λ equality near z ≈ 0.3.

applications_and_observations.topic: Vacuum energy as the source of Λ
applications_and_observations.details: A small Λ could arise from quantum zero-point energy, modelled as a fluid with p = -ρ; its constant density guarantees late-time domination in any expanding universe.
Anti-de Sitter space's timelike boundary makes it the arena for a duality between bulk quantum gravity and a boundary conformal field theory; flagged as an active research area.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Signature (+,-,-,-) with geometric units G = c = 1, so ds² = dt² - R²(...) and density appears as 8πρ.
G_ab - Λg_ab = 8πT_ab (13.5), so Λ > 0 is repulsive in Friedmann's equation and a constant-curvature vacuum has Λ = -3K.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Combined with (24.52) this implies de Sitter (Λ > 0) has K = -1/α² in this convention; the book nevertheless calls K > 0 the de Sitter case.

notation_and_conventions.convention: R(t) denotes the scale factor throughout; R also denotes the Ricci scalar in K = R/12 and R_abcd the Riemann tensor.
C = (8/3)πρR³ for dust; D = (8/3)πρR⁴ for radiation.
notation_and_conventions.notes: C is reused in (25.37) for the constant ρR⁴, and the text's 'C = (8/3)πD' should read D = (8/3)πC.

notation_and_conventions.item: Hubble and de Sitter time scales
notation_and_conventions.convention: α = (3/Λ)^{1/2} in §25.4; T_0 (constant Hubble time) in the steady-state and horizon sections; T_0 is also the radius of the de Sitter and AdS hyperboloids.
notation_and_conventions.notes: With α = T_0 all three agree.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Roman numerals I, II, III for k = -1, 0, +1 and lower-case (i)-(v) with letters (a)-(c) for sub-cases, e.g. III(iic) Eddington-Lemaître, III(iiib) bouncing.
(û, v̂, ŵ, x̂, ŷ, ẑ) are Cartesian coordinates on the flat five-dimensional embedding space; t̂ is the global time on the hyperboloid, distinct from the flat-slicing time t.

notation_and_conventions.item: Radial coordinate χ and function f(χ)
notation_and_conventions.convention: RW metric written dt² - R²[dχ² + f²(χ)dΩ²] with f = χ, sin χ, sinh χ; for AdS χ is instead the compactified radial coordinate.
notation_and_conventions.notes: The text gives χ up to 2π for k = +1; the correct range is 0 to π.

notation_and_conventions.convention: t', r' denote time and polar angle on the Einstein static cylinder (18.27); in §25.11 r' is identified with χ.
τ is the reception time of a signal in §25.7 but conformal time dτ = dt/R in §25.10.
𝒥⁺, 𝒥⁻ (scri) with i⁺, i⁻, i⁰ for timelike and spatial infinity; the extraction renders script I as J.
notation_and_conventions.notes: In Figs 25.14 and 25.15 the big bang and crunch surfaces are also labelled with 𝒥⁻/𝒥⁺ though they are singularities, not infinity.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Called 'flat five-dimensional Euclidean space' in the text but carrying indefinite metrics: (+,-,-,-,-) for de Sitter and (+,+,-,-,-) for anti-de Sitter.
notation_and_conventions.notes: The Fig. 25.11 caption correctly says five-dimensional Minkowski space-time.

notable.summary: Analyse Newtonian motion of a test particle in a straight channel toward a fixed mass, find where its velocity vanishes, write the energy equation and compare the possible motions with Friedmann's equation.
notable.why_notable: Supplies the physical intuition behind the qualitative F(R) method.

notable.summary: Check the time-shift-plus-rescaling symmetry of the flat de Sitter metric and verify that the given transformation reproduces the time part of its static form.
notable.why_notable: Hands-on confirmation that the expansion of de Sitter is a coordinate effect.

notable.summary: From the Robertson-Walker metric compute the Ricci scalar of a constant-time slice and show it equals 6k/R².
notable.why_notable: Underpins the steady-state argument that observable curvature forces k = 0.

notable.summary: Verify the reception time of signals from a comoving source near the de Sitter horizon and its geodesic distance.

difficulty.notes: The first half (§25.1-25.6) is calculus-level ODE work and accessible, though several misprints ((25.1), p = 3ρ, the constants C and D) can derail a careful reader. The second half moves quickly into global structure: embeddings in indefinite-signature 5-spaces, conformal compactification and horizon taxonomy, with many results asserted ('it can be shown') and figures carrying much of the argument. Heavy reliance on Chapters 18 and 24. Equation misprints cluster in §25.7-25.11 and there is a sign inconsistency in the naming of K.

teaching_gems.gem: Reading cosmic history off Ṙ² = F(R): the dominant term at small R gives the universal big bang law, zeros of F give turning points, and the dominant term at large R gives the ultimate fate.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Replaces fourteen separate integrations with one reusable reasoning pattern that also works for radiation and multi-component models.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Potential-plot plus R(t) linked view with draggable parameters and highlighted dominant term in each regime.

teaching_gems.gem: One tabular grid of sketches covering every (k, Λ) case, labelled so later text can say 'models I(i), II(i), III(i), III(iic), III(iiib) all tend to de Sitter'.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Gives learners a map of the whole solution space and a vocabulary to refer to it.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Interactive classification table where each cell animates its universe and links to the parameter-plane explorer.

teaching_gems.gem: Two-line demonstration of why Einstein needed Λ: with R constant, the static Friedmann equations force negative pressure unless Λ is added.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A historically pivotal decision reduces to a transparent algebraic check.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Sliders for Λ, k and a with live readouts of ρ and p; region where both are non-negative is highlighted, collapsing to the Einstein static point.

teaching_gems.gem: Unmasking de Sitter's expansion as a coordinate effect by transforming to a static form.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Forces learners to separate coordinate appearance from geometry, a recurring GR lesson, in a cosmological setting where intuitions are strong.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Same spacetime drawn in two coordinate grids (comoving and static) with a morph animation between them.

teaching_gems.gem: Deriving the steady-state metric purely from the demand that observables (spatial curvature, Hubble rate) be time-independent.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Shows how a symmetry principle plus an observability argument fixes a geometry without solving field equations.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Step-through proof cards with toggles showing what goes wrong if k ≠ 0 or H varies.

teaching_gems.gem: Getting the horizon as the t_0 → ∞ limit of an explicit past light cone, then tracking reception time, redshift and recession speed of a source approaching it.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Connects an abstract causal definition to concrete observables that diverge, which is memorable and testable.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Horizon crossing simulator with live plots of τ, z and dl/dt.

teaching_gems.gem: The explorer who draws the curtain: seeing beyond a horizon is possible but reporting back is not.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A single story conveys observer dependence, reality of hidden events and one-way causal access.

teaching_gems.gem: Horizon existence predicted from the causal character of 𝒥⁻ and 𝒥⁺ (spacelike or null) in conformal diagrams.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Turns horizon questions into a quick glance at a diagram, generalising across spacetimes.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Boundary-type toggles on a schematic Penrose diagram, with particle and event horizons appearing and disappearing.

teaching_gems.gem: Picturing de Sitter as a hyperboloid and showing that the familiar exponential coordinates cover exactly half of it, then seeing the steady-state model's past incompleteness in the Penrose square.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Embedding plus conformal diagram gives two complementary global views of the same fact.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Linked 3D hyperboloid and 2D Penrose square: selecting a region or geodesic in one highlights it in the other.

teaching_gems.gem: Same Gudermannian substitution applied to time (de Sitter) or radius (AdS) decides whether infinity is spacelike or timelike.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Highlights a structural symmetry between the two maximally symmetric spacetimes and explains AdS's 'box' character.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Slider mixing between dS and AdS compactifications on the Einstein static cylinder.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The printed (25.1) has ΛṘ/3 in place of ΛR²/3, and the inline equation at the start of §25.2 has Ṙ where Ṙ² is meant.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The master equation of the chapter appears dimensionally inconsistent at first sight.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Always present Ṙ² = C/R + ΛR²/3 - k and check against (25.3) and (24.60).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: R_m for Λ < 0 (and R = C for k = +1) is described as a 'local minimum', but it is where expansion stops: the maximum of R(t).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think the model bounces off a minimum radius.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Say 'turning point, maximum radius' and show it on a plot.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The text writes p = 3ρ (in §25.5 and §25.12) for radiation, contradicting (25.35) 3p = ρ; and sets C = (8/3)πD, which contradicts (25.39).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Doing the algebra with p = 3ρ gives ρ ∝ R^{-12}; the constants will not match.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use p = ρ/3 and D = (8/3)πρR⁴ consistently; avoid reusing C for radiation.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Equation misprints in the horizon section: (25.48) repeats t_0 in both exponentials and (25.55) omits the division by T_0 in the exponent.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The horizon limit and recession velocity cannot be reproduced from the printed forms.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Sign inconsistency for constant curvature: with the book's field equations and signature, (25.58) and (24.52) imply de Sitter has K = -1/α² < 0, yet the text labels K > 0 as de Sitter and K < 0 as anti-de Sitter. Its 'positive curvature' matches the −+++ convention or refers to the 3-sphere slices.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: A careful learner computing R for de Sitter will get a negative scalar and think they erred.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State explicitly that the sign of K depends on signature conventions; identify spaces by the sign of Λ.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: AdS embedding misprints: (25.64) has -û for -û², (25.67) has a stray 'n', and both embedding spaces are called Euclidean although they have indefinite signature. Later references to '(25.68)' in §25.9 and §25.11 should point to (25.59) and to (25.62)/(25.67), and (25.72) has cosh²(t'/T_0) for cosh²(t̂/T_0).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Confusion when checking embeddings or following equation references.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use corrected forms; label spaces as pseudo-Euclidean with explicit signature.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: For k = +1 the text says χ runs to 2π (should be π) and that conformal time lies in (0, π). For dust with Λ = 0, R = C sin²θ and t = C(θ - sin θ cos θ) give τ = 2θ ∈ (0, 2π). Fig. 25.15 is drawn wider than tall, whereas the correct dust diagram is twice as tall as wide.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Misses the neat fact that light emitted at the bang circles the closed universe exactly once before the crunch, and mis-sizes the Penrose rectangle.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Present τ ∈ (0, 2π) for dust (π for radiation) and redraw the rectangle with correct proportions.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Several internal references say 'Chapter 25' for material in Chapter 26 (dark energy, thermal history, inflation).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers search this chapter in vain.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Fig. 25.18's left panel uses coordinates z and t (a Poincaré-type patch of AdS) that the text never introduces.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The figure cannot be interpreted from the text.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Either explain Poincaré coordinates ds² = (T_0²/z²)(dt² - dz² - dx² - dy²) or drop the panel.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The closing section calls the inflaton's matter content 'dark energy' and writes the vacuum energy-momentum tensor as Λg_ab without the 1/(8π).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Conflates early-universe inflation with late-time acceleration and introduces a factor error.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Reserve 'dark energy' for the present accelerating component; write T_ab = (Λ/8π)g_ab.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Horizons in §25.8 are defined only pictorially; no formula for the particle horizon distance or conditions for its existence in terms of R(t).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners cannot compute whether a given model has horizons.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add χ_ph = ∫dt/R from 0 and χ_eh = ∫dt/R to ∞, with convergence tests for power-law and exponential R.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Stability of the Einstein static universe and the physical mechanism of steady-state matter creation are not discussed; the observational case against steady state is only asserted.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may overrate the static model or not know why steady state failed.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add a perturbation argument using the F(R) picture and briefly cite CMB and radio-source-count evidence (Chapter 26).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Several key results are only asserted: the k = -1 conformal region, inextendibility of RW, the three Λ = Λ_c solutions, and the 'kink' mechanism.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Advanced learners have no route to verify; novices may memorise rather than understand.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Provide numerical integration demos and short derivations (e.g. R̈ = 0 at R³ = 3C/(2Λ)).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The comparison 'R ∝ t^{1/2} is a more rapid expansion than t^{2/3}' is ambiguous without fixing normalisation.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners might think radiation universes expand faster at all times.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Compare at equal H: radiation universes are younger (t = 1/(2H) vs 2/(3H)) because they decelerate more.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Big bang and crunch surfaces are labelled 𝒥⁻ and 𝒥⁺ in Figs 25.14 and 25.15, the symbols used elsewhere for null infinity.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Blurs the distinction between singular boundaries and infinity.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Label singularities separately (e.g. wavy line) and reserve scri for infinity.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The 'open/closed topology' statements assume the simplest global topology for each k.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think curvature alone decides finiteness.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Note that flat and hyperbolic spaces admit compact quotients.

tutor_notes: Open with: 'If you know how fast the universe is expanding today and what it contains, can you predict its whole history?' Then show that Friedmann's equation is a one-dimensional energy equation.
Before any integrals, have the learner sketch R(t) using only the dominance argument (C/R at small R, ΛR²/3 at large R, zeros of F); then reveal the exact solutions as confirmation.
Correct the misprint in (25.1) immediately and flag the p = 3ρ typo before the radiation section, so learners trust their algebra.
Use Exercise 25.7 (particle in a channel) as the bridge for learners with mechanics background; for others, use a ball thrown upward: escape, marginal, fall back.
Check understanding: 'Which models with k = +1 expand for ever?' (Λ > Λ_c, and the Eddington-Lemaître case). 'Can a flat universe recollapse?' (yes, if Λ < 0).
For the Einstein static universe ask the learner to set Ṙ = R̈ = 0 themselves; then ask what happens if R is nudged slightly larger, to motivate instability.
When presenting de Sitter, ask 'Is this universe changing?' before showing the static coordinates; use it as a lesson on coordinate versus invariant statements.
For horizons, first draw the past light cone of a finite t_0, then let t_0 grow on screen; ask the learner to predict what the limit surface looks like.

Common question: 'If the galaxy recedes at the speed of light at the horizon, doesn't that break relativity?' Answer: proper-distance rate of change on a cosmic time slice is not a local velocity; local light cones are respected.
Common question: 'Will we see galaxies disappear?' Answer: they fade and redshift without limit; we never see them cross.

Distinguish particle horizon (what we could have seen so far, set by the past) from event horizon (what we will ever see, set by the future); link each to the shape of the Penrose diagram's bottom and top edges.
When introducing the hyperboloid, remind learners that the embedding space has a minus sign, so the 'waist' is not a bottleneck in a Euclidean sense; show light cones on the surface.
For conformal diagrams, stress that only light-cone structure is preserved; sizes of regions are not physical, but whether boundaries are spacelike, null or timelike is.
Point out the K sign convention issue if the learner is computing curvature; recommend classifying by the sign of Λ.
Finish by asking the learner to narrate the four-era history and justify its order from ρ ∝ R^{-4}, R^{-3}, R^0; then signpost Chapter 26 for real data.
